lectures.title: Lecture 1: Lecture 1: Introduction to Psychology and Society

questions.q: What is the primary focus of Psychology of AI as an interdisciplinary field?
options: Developing more efficient AI algorithms
Examining how people perceive, trust, and collaborate with AI systems
Replacing human workers with AI technology
Maximizing corporate profits from AI investments
Preventing all AI development and deployment
questions.explain: Psychology of AI bridges cognitive psychology, human factors engineering, HCI, and neuroscience to examine how people interact with and are affected by AI. The field focuses on human perception, trust, and collaboration rather than algorithmic development or replacement.

questions.q: According to the lecture, which of the following best describes the relationship between trustworthiness, trust, and trusting behaviour?
options: They are three names for the same psychological concept
Trustworthiness is subjective, while trust and trusting behaviour are objective
Trustworthiness is an objective attribute; trust is a psychological state; trusting behaviour is the actual act of reliance
They exist only in human relationships, not in human-AI contexts
Trustworthiness determines behaviour directly without any psychological mediation
questions.explain: The notes clearly distinguish these three concepts: trustworthiness is objective (does the system deserve trust?), trust is psychological (do users perceive it as trustworthy?), and trusting behaviour is behavioural (do users actually rely on it?). This distinction is explicitly flagged as an exam trap.

questions.q: Research by Choung et al. (2023) and others shows that trust in AI predicts which two outcomes?
options: Faster internet speeds and lower costs
Acceptance of AI and intention to use AI
Government regulation and compliance
Improved algorithm transparency
Reduced anxiety and workplace conflict
questions.explain: The lecture explicitly states that trust in AI predicts acceptance of AI and intention to use AI, supported by Choung et al. (2023). This is foundational to understanding why trust matters in AI adoption.

questions.q: Which three components constitute AI trustworthiness according to Bedue & Fritzsche (2021)?
options: Transparency, explainability, and reliability
Ability, integrity, and benevolence
Speed, accuracy, and cost-effectiveness
Data quality, certifications, and privacy
Intelligence, power, and efficiency
questions.explain: Bedue & Fritzsche identify ability (knowledge, quality), integrity (ethics, regulation), and benevolence (social responsibility, sustainability) as the three key components. While other factors like transparency and explainability matter, these three are the core constituting components.

questions.q: In Li et al. (2024)'s integrative framework, trustor factors include all of the following EXCEPT:
options: Self-efficacy
Emotional experience
Robustness
Hedonic motivation
Sense of control
questions.explain: Robustness is a trustee (AI system) factor, not a trustor (user) factor. The framework separates trustor factors (user characteristics like self-efficacy and emotional experience) from trustee factors (system characteristics like robustness and competence).

questions.q: What does the lecture suggest about humans' perception of AI compared to other technologies?
options: Humans judge AI purely on functional performance metrics
Humans tend to treat AI as social actors and assess warmth and competence
Humans ignore emotional and social dimensions when using AI
Humans evaluate AI entirely through economic cost-benefit analysis
Humans view AI identically to how they view conventional tools
questions.explain: McKee et al. (2023) found that humans assess AI's warmth (friendliness, sincerity) and competence (intelligence, power), treating AI as social actors rather than mere tools. This is a distinctive aspect of AI perception compared to other technologies.

questions.q: According to Li et al. (2025), which two factors were most influential in affecting trust in AI?
options: Data quality and certification standards
Warmth and competence perceptions
Cost and performance metrics
Government regulation and transparency
Speed and processing power
questions.explain: The lecture explicitly states that in a China study, warmth and competence were the two most influential factors affecting trust in AI, alongside anthropomorphism, robustness, and participant characteristics.

questions.q: What is a key distinction between virtual assistants and chess-playing AI systems in terms of perceived warmth and competence?
options: Virtual assistants score higher on both warmth and competence
Chess systems are perceived as warmer but less competent
Virtual assistants are perceived as warmer but less competent
They are perceived identically in both dimensions
Competence cannot be measured for chess systems
questions.explain: The lecture notes that virtual assistants and smart vacuums are perceived as warmer, while chess-playing systems and video recommenders are perceived as more competent. Warmth and competence are independent dimensions.

questions.q: In Cheng et al. (2026)'s metaphor study, which metaphors increased significantly after ChatGPT's introduction?
options: Search engine, computer, mirror, and synthesizer
Assistant, friend, robot, child, teacher, and god
Calculator, database, and tool
Machine, algorithm, and system
Servant, slave, and worker
questions.explain: The study collected over 12,000 metaphor responses and found increasing metaphors (r > 0.3) of assistant, friend, robot, child, teacher, and god — reflecting increased perception of human-likeness and warmth after ChatGPT's introduction.

questions.q: What is the performance paradox in the context of AI-assisted work?
options: AI systems are always superior to humans in every task
AI improves immediate outcomes but may reduce critical thinking and skill development
Workers refuse to use AI even when it increases productivity
Performance improvements are evenly distributed across all worker demographics
Productivity gains are temporary and disappear after one week
questions.explain: The performance paradox describes how AI can improve immediate outputs while potentially reducing critical thinking, metacognitive monitoring, skill development, and unaided performance later — a trade-off that users may not recognize.

questions.q: In Noy & Zhang (2023)'s ChatGPT study, what was the effect size for time reduction on professional tasks?
questions.explain: The lecture reports that ChatGPT users completed professional tasks 40% faster with a treatment effect of -0.75 SDs on time taken and +0.41 SDs on grade (quality). The negative SD indicates faster completion.

questions.q: What does cognitive offloading involve?
options: Forcing workers to retire early
Transferring workplace stresses to family members
Delegating cognitive tasks to external resources like AI to reduce mental demand
Avoiding all use of technology in decision-making
Creating backup copies of computer files
questions.explain: Cognitive offloading is the delegation of cognitive tasks to external resources to reduce mental demand. Ideally it frees resources for higher-level thinking, but it can become problematic if combined with automation bias.

questions.q: In Gerlich (2025)'s cross-sectional study, what was the correlation between AI tool use and cognitive offloading?
questions.explain: Gerlich found that AI tool use correlated positively with cognitive offloading (r = +0.72), and cognitive offloading negatively correlated with critical thinking (r = -0.75). The chain shows how AI use can indirectly reduce critical thinking.

questions.q: What is automation bias and why is it a critical risk?
options: An automatic feature that prevents user errors
The tendency to over-rely on automated systems and cease independent verification, risking poor decisions in high-stakes domains
A type of computer malfunction that occurs randomly
A beneficial cognitive shortcut that saves mental effort
A preference for one automation brand over another
questions.explain: Automation bias leads people to perceive AI as more objective and reliable than humans, causing them to cease verification and independent thinking. This is particularly dangerous in high-stakes domains like healthcare or finance.

questions.q: Which AI interaction persona achieved the highest quiz score in Shen & Tamkin (2026)'s programming study?
options: AI Delegation (39%)
Progressive AI Reliance (35%)
Iterative AI Debugging (31%)
Generation-Then-Comprehension (86%)
Hybrid Code-Explanation (50%)
questions.explain: The study identified six personas with vastly different outcomes. Generation-Then-Comprehension achieved 86% quiz score with 24 minutes, while pure delegation personas scored much lower (31-39%), showing that cognitively engaging usage patterns preserve skills.

questions.q: What was the impact of GenAI on task performance in Wu et al. (2025)'s research?
options: GenAI enhanced solo performance but not collaborative performance
GenAI enhanced immediate performance but augmentation did not persist in subsequent solo tasks
GenAI had no effect on either immediate or delayed performance
GenAI only affected motivation without changing actual task performance
GenAI improved all aspects of performance permanently
questions.explain: Wu et al. found that while GenAI enhanced immediate task performance, this benefit did not persist when users later worked solo. Performance gains were temporary and tied to the presence of the AI tool.

questions.q: According to the lecture, what is collaborative AI literacy?
options: The ability to teach AI systems about human culture
A certification program for AI developers
Competencies enabling individuals to critically evaluate collaborative AI tools and use them effectively
Knowledge of how to build AI systems
The skill of speaking multiple programming languages
questions.explain: Sidra & Mason (2026) define collaborative AI literacy as competencies that enable individuals to critically evaluate collaborative AI tools, communicate and coordinate with them effectively, and use them well.

questions.q: What dimension of AI anxiety is NOT mentioned in the lecture's table?
options: Privacy violation
Bias behaviour
Job replacement
Environmental impact
Lack of transparency
questions.explain: The table lists eight dimensions: privacy violation, bias behaviour, job replacement, learning difficulty, existential risk, against ethics, artificial consciousness, and lack of transparency. Environmental impact is not listed as a dimension.

questions.q: In Noy & Zhang (2023)'s study on ChatGPT use, which statement accurately describes the effect on user attitudes?
options: Users became fearful and reduced their engagement with AI
Users reported higher job replacement concerns but also higher excitement and optimism about AI
Users showed consistent negative or positive attitudes but not both
AI use eliminated all forms of anxiety
Users became indifferent to both benefits and risks
questions.explain: The study demonstrates ambivalence: ChatGPT users simultaneously reported higher worry about job replacement (+0.266 SDs) AND higher excitement (+0.206 SDs) and optimism (+0.379 SDs). This is not contradiction but coexistence of both attitudes.

questions.q: What does Dong et al. (2026)'s cross-national study suggest about AI fears?
options: Fear of AI is universal across all countries and occupations
Fear of AI is occupation-specific and driven by mismatch between necessary traits and AI potential
Fear of AI is only present in developed countries
Fear of AI is unrelated to any psychological or cultural factors
All countries show identical patterns of fear toward specific occupations
questions.explain: Dong et al. found that fear of AI is occupation-specific and varies across countries, driven by the mismatch between traits deemed necessary for an occupation and perceived AI potential. Saudi Arabia showed high fear of Religious AI while Japan showed low fear of Careworker AI.

questions.q: Which two disciplines does Psychology of AI NOT explicitly bridge according to the lecture?
options: Cognitive psychology and human-computer interaction
Neuroscience and political science
Human factors engineering and neuroscience
Psychology and philosophy
Cognitive psychology and neuroscience
questions.explain: The lecture states Psychology of AI bridges cognitive psychology, human factors engineering, human-computer interaction, and neuroscience. Political science and philosophy are not listed as core disciplines being bridged.

questions.q: In the trust process described in the lecture, which stage occurs AFTER impression formation?
options: Actual trustworthiness
Impression formation
Intention to rely
Trusting use
Perception formation
questions.explain: The four-stage process flows from actual trustworthiness → impression formation → intention to rely → trusting use. Intention to rely comes after impression formation and assesses willingness based on perceived risks and stakes.

questions.q: How did attributions of human-likeness change in the year after ChatGPT's introduction according to Cheng et al. (2026)?
options: They decreased significantly
They increased significantly
They remained stable
They became negatively correlated with warmth
They showed no consistent pattern
questions.explain: The study found that participants' attributions of human-likeness and warmth increased significantly in the year after ChatGPT was introduced, reflecting growing perception of AI as more human-like.

questions.q: According to research on productivity gains, which group benefited most from ChatGPT access in Noy & Zhang (2023)?
options: Only workers with advanced degrees
Participants with lower initial grades (potential to level productivity inequality)
Experienced workers with decades of experience
Full-time employees only
Participants from English-speaking countries only
questions.explain: Noy & Zhang found that ChatGPT had potential to level productivity inequality because participants with lower initial grades benefited MORE from ChatGPT access, suggesting AI can reduce performance gaps.

questions.q: What implication does the lecture draw about the relationship between immediate performance gains and long-term learning?
options: They are always positively correlated
They may be in tension; designers must balance immediate gains against long-term costs to learning and development
Long-term learning always improves immediate performance
There is no relationship between the two
Immediate gains always persist long-term
questions.explain: The lecture emphasizes that designers of AI tools must balance immediate performance gains against long-term costs to learning and development, a core implication of the performance paradox and skill atrophy findings.

questions.q: Which research finding most directly contradicts the assumption that competent AI systems are always perceived as warm?
options: Li et al. (2024) on trust dimensions
McKee et al. (2023) on AI perception differences across system types
Cheng et al. (2026) on metaphor shifts
Noy & Zhang (2023) on productivity gains
Gerlich (2025) on cognitive offloading
questions.explain: McKee et al. found that chess-playing systems and video recommenders are perceived as more competent but LESS warm, while virtual assistants are warmer but less competent. This directly demonstrates that warmth and competence are independent dimensions.

questions.q: What does the lecture suggest about the future topics within the Psychology of AI subject?
options: Only technical improvements to AI systems
AI tools in research, therapeutic applications, digital mental health, AI ethics, and relationships with AI (chatbots and companions)
Exclusively economic implications of AI
Only government policy and regulation
Purely philosophical questions without practical application
questions.explain: The lecture explicitly lists future topics: AI tools in research, how humans think and AI development, AI applications in therapeutic and mental health settings, ethics in AI use, and relationships with AI including chatbots and companions.

questions.q: In the context of skill atrophy, why does usage pattern matter according to Shen & Tamkin (2026)?
options: Only cognitively engaging patterns preserve and develop skills
All usage patterns equally harm skill development
Non-engaging usage patterns always lead to better outcomes
Usage patterns do not matter at all
Skill preservation is unrelated to AI use
questions.explain: Shen & Tamkin found that cognitively engaging usage patterns (like Generation-Then-Comprehension with 86% quiz score) yielded much higher skill retention than passive delegation patterns (31-39% scores), showing that HOW users interact with AI matters for learning.

questions.q: According to the lecture, what shift occurred in how people refer to AI after ChatGPT's introduction?
options: Increased use of technical terms like algorithm and database
Shift from tool metaphors (search engine, computer) toward social metaphors (friend, teacher, god)
No meaningful change in language or metaphor use
People stopped using any metaphors at all
Exclusively increased use of negative metaphors
questions.explain: Cheng et al. (2026) found that decreasing metaphors (r < -0.3) included search engine and computer, while increasing metaphors (r > 0.3) included assistant, friend, robot, child, teacher, and god — reflecting a shift toward more human-like conceptualizations.

questions.q: What is the relationship between collaborative AI metacognition and the performance paradox?
options: They are completely unrelated concepts
Metacognition (planning, monitoring, reflection) may mitigate paradox by sustaining critical thinking and awareness during AI use
Metacognition always eliminates all performance improvements
The paradox only applies to users with low metacognition
Metacognition makes the paradox worse
questions.explain: The lecture suggests that collaborative AI metacognition — the ability to enhance awareness and control of one's thinking through planning, monitoring, and reflection — is a mitigation strategy for the performance paradox, helping users maintain critical thinking while using AI.

lectures.title: Lecture 2: Are You More Introverted or Extraverted?

questions.q: Which of the following best describes a personality trait according to trait theory?
options: A psychological disorder diagnosed by a clinician
An enduring predisposition that characterizes a person and tends to vary across individuals
A temporary mood state that changes daily
A learned behavior acquired only through social reinforcement
A fixed category determined entirely by genetics
questions.explain: Personality is defined as enduring predispositions that characterize a person and vary across individuals (personality-definition). The incorrect options confuse personality with disorders, moods, learned-only behaviors, or purely genetic determinism—none of which capture the trait theory approach.

questions.q: What is the primary limitation of trait theories in explaining personality?
options: They are too focused on environmental factors
They describe personality structure but do not explain what causes personality
They only apply to Western populations
They rely exclusively on projective methods
They cannot measure individual differences
questions.explain: Trait theories describe and compare personality structure but do NOT explain the causes of personality (trait-theory-limits)—this is the critical exam trap. Description and causal explanation are different. The other options misrepresent trait theory's actual scope and methods.

questions.q: Factor analysis applied to personality trait terms consistently reveals which structure?
options: Three major trait dimensions
A five-factor pattern underlying personality variation
Ten independent dimensions with no intercorrelation
A single general personality factor
Six trait factors accounting for all variance
questions.explain: Factor analysis of trait terms in dictionaries and literature consistently reveals a five-factor structure (factor-analysis). This statistical method identifies which variables cluster together, revealing the underlying basic traits that form the basis of personality description.

questions.q: In the Big Five (OCEAN) model, which trait is characterized by orderliness, self-discipline, and reliability?
options: Openness
Conscientiousness
Extraversion
Agreeableness
Neuroticism
questions.explain: Conscientiousness (big-five-overview) is the Big Five trait describing organization, reliability, and self-discipline. High scorers are organized, hardworking, and persevering. This is distinct from Openness (imagination) or Extraversion (sociability).

questions.q: Which Big Five trait shows the strongest empirical link to salesperson job performance?
options: Openness to new ideas
Conscientiousness and reliability
Extraversion in social situations
Agreeableness and cooperation
Low Neuroticism
questions.explain: Extraversion is particularly important for salesperson performance (big-five-real-world, Furnham & Fudge, 2008), reflecting the social and persuasive nature of sales roles. While other traits matter for general job performance, Extraversion specifically predicts sales success.

questions.q: What was the finding regarding Extraversion and COVID-19 sheltering-in-place behavior?
options: High Extraversion was positively related to staying home
Extraversion was unrelated to sheltering behavior
High Extraversion was negatively related to staying home
Low Extraversion predicted longer lockdown compliance
Extraversion predicted infection rates but not isolation
questions.explain: Extraversion was negatively related to sheltering-in-place during COVID-19—more extraverted individuals were less likely to stay home (big-five-real-world, Gotz et al., 2021). This is a key exam trap: Openness and Neuroticism were positively related to staying home, opposite to Extraversion.

questions.q: According to Matz et al. (2017), how much more effective were personality-matched ads compared to non-personalized ads?
options: Up to 10% more clicks and 15% more purchases
Up to 25% more clicks and 30% more purchases
Up to 40% more clicks and up to 50% more purchases
Up to 60% more clicks and 70% more purchases
No significant difference in effectiveness
questions.explain: Personality-matched ads resulted in up to 40% more clicks and up to 50% more purchases compared to non-personalized ads in a study of 3.5 million Facebook users (big-five-real-world, Matz et al., 2017). This demonstrates real-world commercial value of personality assessment.

questions.q: How many traits does the HEXACO model include, and what is the unique sixth trait?
options: Five traits; the sixth is merely a reformulation of Conscientiousness
Six traits; the sixth is Dominance
Six traits; the sixth is Honesty-Humility, relevant to ethical and power-seeking behavior
Seven traits; the sixth is Achievement-Striving
Six traits; the sixth is Anxiety
questions.explain: HEXACO has six traits; five are variants of the Big Five, and the unique sixth is Honesty-Humility (hexaco-model)—which characterizes sincere versus self-centered and manipulative individuals. Low Honesty-Humility shows the strongest negative relation with workplace deviance.

questions.q: Which HEXACO trait shows the strongest negative relationship with workplace deviance behaviors?
options: Low Extraversion
Low Openness
Low Conscientiousness
Low Honesty-Humility
Low Agreeableness
questions.explain: Low Honesty-Humility is most strongly negatively related to workplace deviance—including stealing, damaging property, and harassment (hexaco-model, Pletzer et al., 2019). This is a critical exam trap: students may confuse this with low Agreeableness, which is less predictive.

questions.q: What is the key difference between reliability and validity in personality testing?
options: Reliability measures cultural appropriateness; validity measures test cost
Reliability is consistency across items and time; validity is whether the test measures what it claims
Validity ensures the test is given fairly; reliability ensures all respondents get the same results
Reliability requires a computer; validity requires human judgment
They are synonymous terms used interchangeably in psychometrics
questions.explain: Reliability (test-evaluation-criteria) is consistency of responses across items and repeated assessments. Validity is the extent to which the measure assesses what it claims to measure—criterion validity specifically means the test predicts trait-related behavior. Both require empirical evidence.

questions.q: Which position level most frequently uses personality tests in hiring decisions?
options: Hourly workers and entry-level positions
Individual contributors and specialists
Middle management positions
Executive-level positions
All levels equally
questions.explain: Personality tests are most often used for high-level positions—executive positions receive personality assessments more frequently than middle managers, individual contributors, or hourly workers (test-evaluation-criteria, SHRM, 2017). Higher stakes and complexity drive more extensive assessment.

questions.q: Which of the following is NOT a threat to validity in self-report personality tests?
options: Social desirability bias
Self-enhancement bias
Inaccessible self-concept
Excessive question length causing fatigue
All of these are threats to validity
questions.explain: The main threats to self-report test validity (self-report-tests) are inaccurate or inaccessible self-concept and biases like social desirability and self-enhancement. Excessive question length (excessive fatigue) is not explicitly mentioned as a primary threat in the lecture materials, making it the exception.

questions.q: What is the primary assumption underlying projective personality tests?
options: Respondents lie about their true personality
Important thoughts and motives operate outside conscious awareness
Personality is determined entirely by genetics
Projective tests measure only current mood states
Ambiguous stimuli have universal symbolic meanings
questions.explain: Projective tests assume that important thoughts, feelings, and motives operate outside conscious awareness (projective-tests). The projective hypothesis (Frank, 1949) posits that interpreting ambiguous stimuli reveals what the test-taker 'cannot or will not say.'

questions.q: Which of the following is an example of a projective personality test?
options: Self-report questionnaire with Likert-scale responses
Computer analysis of Facebook Likes
Rorschach Test using inkblots
Behavioral observation in naturalistic settings
Structured interview with standardized questions
questions.explain: The Rorschach Test (projective-tests) uses symmetrical inkblots and asks test-takers what they see. The Thematic Apperception Test (TAT) is another classic example. Both rely on interpretation of ambiguous stimuli, distinguishing them from self-report and automatic assessment methods.

questions.q: What is a major threat to the reliability of projective personality tests?
options: Low internal consistency among items
Lack of statistical standardization
Subjectivity in interpreting and scoring responses
Respondents' lack of motivation to answer honestly
Overly long test duration
questions.explain: Projective tests face threats to reliability (projective-tests) because responses could be inconsistent and their interpretation could be highly subjective. Unlike self-report tests, standardized scoring is difficult, and evaluator bias can affect results.

questions.q: According to Wu et al. (2015), approximately how many Facebook Likes are needed for a computer model to match average human accuracy in personality assessment?
options: 40–50 Likes
60–75 Likes
90–100 Likes
150–200 Likes
300+ Likes
questions.explain: With approximately 90–100 Facebook Likes, a computer model matches the accuracy of the average human judge (r = 0.49) in personality assessment (automatic-assessment, Wu et al., 2015). This is notably lower than spouse accuracy (r = 0.58), a key distinction for exam questions.

questions.q: Which of the following statements is accurate regarding computer model accuracy versus human judge accuracy?
options: Computers consistently outperform all human raters including spouses
Computer average (r = 0.56) exceeds spouse accuracy (r = 0.58)
Computer average (r = 0.56) and spouse accuracy (r = 0.58) are comparable but computers still fall short
Computers are less accurate than work colleagues (r = 0.27)
Human raters universally perform better than automatic assessment methods
questions.explain: Computer average accuracy (r = 0.56) closely approaches but does not exceed spouse accuracy (r = 0.58) (automatic-assessment). This is an exam trap—claiming computers outperform all human raters is incorrect. Spouse ratings remain the most accurate human comparison.

questions.q: Which digital signals are most predictive of Big Five personality traits according to Park et al. (2015)?
options: Music playlist selections alone
Facebook Likes, status updates, spending records, and pictures
Only profile bio text
Search history exclusively
Login frequency and time spent online
questions.explain: Multiple digital footprint signals predict Big Five traits (automatic-assessment, Park et al., 2015): Facebook Likes are most predictive for Openness and Conscientiousness, while statuses, spending records, Flickr pictures, and music preferences also contribute. No single source is sufficient.

questions.q: What is the defining characteristic of a personality type as opposed to a trait dimension?
options: Types are measurable on a continuous scale from low to high
Types imply relative homogeneity within groups and heterogeneity between groups
Types are always more valid than dimensional approaches
Types can be changed through therapy but traits cannot
Types are based on biological neurotransmitters only
questions.explain: Personality types (personality-types) classify individuals into distinct groups and imply homogeneity within a group and heterogeneity between groups—contrasting with dimensional approaches that use continuous scales. This categorical distinction is fundamental.

questions.q: How many dichotomies and resulting personality types does the Myers-Briggs Type Indicator include?
options: Two dichotomies producing 4 types
Three dichotomies producing 8 types
Four dichotomies producing 16 types
Five dichotomies producing 32 types
Four dichotomies producing 12 types
questions.explain: MBTI (mbti) has four dichotomies: E/I (Extraversion/Introversion), S/N (Sensing/Intuition), T/F (Thinking/Feeling), and J/P (Judging/Perceiving), producing 2^4 = 16 personality types. These four dimensions define the familiar four-letter MBTI codes.

questions.q: What is the operational distinction between the Thinking and Feeling dimensions in MBTI?
options: Thinking = fast processing; Feeling = slow processing
Thinking = decisions via logical reasoning; Feeling = decisions based on personal values and social impact
Thinking = intelligence; Feeling = emotional stability
Thinking = introverted; Feeling = extraverted
Thinking = preference for facts; Feeling = preference for symbols
questions.explain: The T/F dichotomy (mbti) contrasts impersonal logical reasoning (Thinking) with decisions based on personal values and impact on others (Feeling). This is distinct from intelligence or emotional stability, and independent of Extraversion/Introversion.

questions.q: According to Randall et al. (2017), how many studies with sufficient quality evidence were found in a systematic review of MBTI reliability and validity?
options: Fewer than 3 studies
7 studies with variable quality, mostly using student samples
15 high-quality studies
30+ peer-reviewed studies
MBTI has never been formally evaluated
questions.explain: A systematic review by Randall et al. (2017) found only 7 studies with sufficient information, variable quality, and 6 of which used only student samples (mbti-criticism). This demonstrates limited empirical support for MBTI despite its popularity.

questions.q: What is the primary statistical evidence against the MBTI type model approach?
options: MBTI shows poor internal consistency within each type
Personality variation follows a bell curve, not distinct bimodal categories
MBTI cannot distinguish between introverts and extraverts
Type models predict behavior worse than random assignment
The four dichotomies are not independent of each other
questions.explain: Personality variation falls on a bell curve (常態分布), not distinct categories (mbti-criticism, Pittenger, 2005)—most people score near the midpoint, not at extremes, contradicting MBTI's categorical type assumptions. Lack of bimodality is the key empirical problem.

questions.q: What false impression does the four-letter MBTI type formula create?
options: That personality is entirely genetically determined
That all 16 types are equally common in the population
Meaningful categorical differences between profiles when no such difference exists
That personality cannot change over the lifespan
That self-report is the only valid assessment method
questions.explain: The four-letter MBTI type formula creates the impression of meaningful differences between profiles when no such categorical boundaries actually exist in continuous personality data (mbti-criticism, Pittenger, 2005). The formula imposes false structure on underlying continuous variation.

questions.q: Which of the following best describes why personality type classification lacks scientific rigor?
options: Type models require expensive assessment tools
Continuous trait distributions do not support categorical boundaries
Type models have never been used in organizational settings
Types cannot be reliably distinguished by self-report methods
Type models are less popular than dimensional models
questions.explain: Personality type classification lacks scientific rigor (mbti-criticism) because the underlying data show continuous distributions (bell curve), not categorical clusters that would support type boundaries. Imposing discrete types on continuous variation violates the data structure.

questions.q: Compared to self-report and projective methods, what is the primary advantage of automatic assessment?
options: It requires no assumptions about test validity
It can be computed directly from digital footprint data without subjective interpretation
It eliminates all bias in personality measurement
It is cheaper than other methods but less accurate
It works equally well across all populations
questions.explain: Automatic assessment's primary advantage (automatic-assessment) is that it can compute personality measures from digital data without requiring respondents to introspect or scoring that depends on subjective interpretation. This differs from projective tests (subjective scoring) and self-report (self-perception biases).

questions.q: Which Big Five trait is most associated with preference for reflective and complex music genres?
options: High Conscientiousness
High Openness
High Extraversion with high Agreeableness
High Neuroticism
Low Agreeableness
questions.explain: Openness is associated with preference for reflective and complex music (e.g., classical, jazz), while Extraversion plus Agreeableness predict preference for energetic and rhythmic music (big-five-real-world, Rentfrow & Gosling, 2003). This demonstrates personality's link to aesthetic preferences.

questions.q: Based on Tett et al. (1991), which combination of Big Five traits predicts the best job performance?
options: High Openness and high Extraversion
High Conscientiousness, low Neuroticism, and high Agreeableness
High Agreeableness and high Conscientiousness only
Low Neuroticism and low Extraversion
High Openness and low Conscientiousness
questions.explain: The combination of high conscientiousness, low neuroticism, and high agreeableness predicts better job performance (big-five-real-world, Tett et al., 1991). This pattern reflects reliability, emotional stability, and cooperativeness—valued across most occupational contexts.

questions.q: What do factor analysis results consistently demonstrate about the structure of personality traits?
options: Personality traits are randomly distributed with no underlying pattern
A coherent five-factor structure emerges across diverse trait samples and populations
Personality varies entirely by culture with no universal structure
Individual traits are completely independent and unrelated
Only four basic traits are necessary to describe all personality variation
questions.explain: Factor analysis applied to diverse personality trait samples consistently reveals a five-factor structure (factor-analysis), suggesting this structure reflects fundamental underlying organization of personality variation. This consistency across methods and populations lends credibility to the Big Five model.

questions.q: How do psychologists distinguish between personality description and personality explanation?
options: Description uses questionnaires; explanation uses interviews
Description identifies what traits exist; explanation addresses what causes those traits
Description applies only to normal populations; explanation applies to clinical disorders
There is no meaningful distinction between description and explanation
Description relies on self-report; explanation relies on biological measures
questions.explain: Personality description (e.g., trait theories) identifies and structures what traits exist and how they vary across individuals (trait-theory-limits), while explanation addresses the causes or origins of those traits. Trait theories excel at description but do not inherently explain causation.

lectures.title: Lecture 3: Is Fearing Birds a Mental Disorder? Phobias and Mental Health

questions.q: Which of the following BEST describes why statistical rarity alone cannot define mental illness?
options: Rare conditions are never serious enough to require treatment
Some rare conditions, like exceptional creativity or athletic ability, are positive and not considered disorders
The rarity of a disorder is only relevant if it causes distress to the individual
Statistical measures are never reliable in psychology
Rare disorders are more likely to be culture-bound syndromes
questions.explain: The notes explicitly state that some rare conditions (exceptional athletic ability, creativity) are not disorders. Statistical rarity is one criterion, but deviance alone cannot define mental illness—deviance, distress, and dysfunction must be considered together.

questions.q: According to the lecture, what are the three key criteria for defining mental illness?
options: Deviance, distress, and dysfunction
Rarity, severity, and treatment response
Biological cause, psychological symptoms, and social impact
Age of onset, duration, and symptom count
Diagnosis, prognosis, and genetic predisposition
questions.explain: The notes clearly identify deviance (statistical rarity), distress (psychological pain), and dysfunction (impairment in functioning) as the three main criteria. None of these criteria alone is sufficient; they must be considered together.

questions.q: What is a culture-bound syndrome, and which of the following is NOT listed as an example in this lecture?
options: Koro, a Southeast Asian anxiety syndrome about genital retraction
Hikikomori, severe social withdrawal found primarily in Japan
Schizophrenia, a widely recognized disorder across all cultures
Both Koro and Hikikomori are culture-bound
Koro is specifically associated with Southeast Asia and parts of Africa
questions.explain: Schizophrenia is a disorder recognized across cultures, not a culture-bound syndrome. The lecture explicitly identifies Koro and Hikikomori as culture-bound syndromes. Culture-bound syndromes are symptoms or conditions specific to one or a limited number of societies.

questions.q: The lecture notes an important distinction regarding when homosexuality was removed from diagnostic manuals. Which statement is CORRECT?
options: Both APA and WHO removed homosexuality in 1973
The APA removed it in 1973; the WHO removed it in 1990
The WHO removed it in 1973; the APA removed it in 1990
Homosexuality is still classified as a disorder in both DSM-5 and ICD-11
Neither the APA nor WHO has officially removed homosexuality from their diagnostic systems
questions.explain: An exam trap in the notes warns not to conflate these dates. The APA removed homosexuality from its diagnostic manual in 1973; the WHO followed later in 1990. This shows how diagnostic boundaries shift over time.

questions.q: Which of the following BEST explains why diagnosis is important in mental health care?
options: It guarantees that a patient will be cured
It identifies the problem, informs treatment planning, and facilitates communication among professionals
It determines whether a person qualifies for disability benefits
It proves that a mental disorder has a biological cause
It ensures that all patients with the same diagnosis receive identical treatment
questions.explain: The notes identify three specific functions of diagnosis: pinpointing the problem, informing treatment design, and facilitating communication among professionals. Diagnosis does not guarantee cure or prove biological causation.

questions.q: How many disorders are included in DSM-5, and who publishes it?
options: 237 disorders, published by the World Health Organization
237 disorders, published by the American Psychiatric Association
Over 500 disorders, published by the American Psychiatric Association
237 disorders, published by the National Institute of Mental Health
Unknown number, published by both APA and WHO jointly
questions.explain: The table in the notes clearly states DSM-5 contains 237 disorders and is published by the American Psychiatric Association (APA). The ICD-11 is published by WHO and is broader, covering all diseases.

questions.q: What is a key difference between DSM-5 and ICD-11 in terms of scope?
options: DSM-5 covers all diseases; ICD-11 covers mental disorders only
DSM-5 covers mental disorders only; ICD-11 covers all diseases and mortality/morbidity statistics
Both systems are identical in scope and content
DSM-5 is used in Asia; ICD-11 is used in Western countries
ICD-11 covers only physical illnesses; DSM-5 covers mental disorders
questions.explain: The comparison table shows DSM-5 focuses on mental disorders only, while ICD-11 includes all diseases and is used for global mortality and morbidity statistics. This is a key difference in their scope and purpose.

questions.q: Which of the following is NOT listed as a chapter category in DSM-5?
options: Neurodevelopmental Disorders
Depressive Disorders and Anxiety Disorders
Schizophrenia Spectrum and Other Psychotic Disorders
Chronic physical illnesses and medical conditions
Personality Disorders and Paraphilic Disorders
questions.explain: The lecture states DSM-5 covers mental disorders only. Chronic physical illnesses and medical conditions are not DSM-5 categories—the list of 10 chapter categories provided does not include medical conditions as a primary diagnostic category.

questions.q: According to the lecture, what tools or methods does a mental health professional use to make a diagnosis?
options: Clinical interview and physical examination only
Psychological testing and diagnostic criteria only
Clinical interview, physical examination, psychological testing, and diagnostic criteria
Only reviewing the patient's medical history
Brain imaging scans and genetic testing exclusively
questions.explain: The notes explicitly list four components of the diagnostic process: clinical interview, physical examination, psychological testing, and diagnostic criteria. All four are used together to reach a diagnosis.

questions.q: For a diagnosis of Major Depressive Disorder (MDD), which statement is CORRECT?
options: Any 5 of the 9 symptoms over 2 weeks is sufficient for diagnosis
5 or more symptoms are required, but at least 1 must be depressed mood OR loss of interest/pleasure
Exactly 5 symptoms, all from the same category, are required
9 symptoms are required, all persisting for at least 4 weeks
Only the first 5 symptoms from the list need to be present
questions.explain: The notes and exam trap both clarify that MDD requires 5+ symptoms (with at least 1 of the first two being either depressed mood or loss of interest/pleasure), persisting over 2 weeks. This is a critical diagnostic rule often tested.

questions.q: Which of the following symptoms is NOT listed in the 9 DSM-5 criteria for Major Depressive Disorder?
options: Loss of interest or pleasure (anhedonia)
Thoughts of death or suicidal ideation
Excessive worry about future events
Insomnia or hypersomnia
Feelings of worthlessness or guilt
questions.explain: Excessive worry about future events is not listed in the MDD criteria. The nine criteria cover mood, anhedonia, appetite/weight, sleep, psychomotor changes, energy, worthlessness/guilt, concentration, and suicidal ideation.

questions.q: Based on DSM-5 data cited in the lecture, what percentage of people with OCD also meet criteria for Major Depressive Disorder?
options: Approximately 25%
Approximately 41%
Approximately 60%
Approximately 75%
Approximately 90%
questions.explain: The notes explicitly state that 41% of people with OCD also meet criteria for MDD. This is an example of comorbidity, where two mental disorders co-occur in the same individual.

questions.q: What does the lecture reveal about comorbidity between depression and anxiety disorders?
options: They rarely occur together; most depressed people do not experience anxiety
Over half of people with MDD also exhibit some form of anxiety disorder, and vice versa
Anxiety always comes before depression in all cases of comorbidity
Comorbidity between depression and anxiety is a new phenomenon not seen in older populations
Only severe cases of depression show comorbidity with anxiety
questions.explain: The notes state that over half of people with a primary depressive disorder also exhibit some anxiety disorder, and the reverse is also true. This demonstrates how common comorbidity is between these two conditions.

questions.q: Which of the following BEST captures what the lecture means by 'medicalization'?
options: The requirement that all mental illness must have a biological cause
The growing number of DSM diagnoses and increasing medication use for psychological problems
The process of replacing therapy with medication in all cases
The invention of new mental disorders by pharmaceutical companies
The requirement that all medical professionals must study psychiatry
questions.explain: The notes define medicalization as the growing number of diagnoses in the DSM and increasing number of people on medications for psychological problems. The concern is that mild and normal disturbances are too easily classified as pathological.

questions.q: What specific change in DSM-5 illustrates the concern about medicalization and the expanding diagnostic boundary?
options: It added 500 new disorder categories
It removed the bereavement exclusion, allowing MDD diagnosis following loss of a loved one if criteria are met
It eliminated all personality disorder diagnoses
It required biological testing for all diagnoses
It removed anxiety disorders from the diagnostic manual
questions.explain: The notes specifically highlight that DSM-5 removed the 'bereavement exclusion,' meaning grief after loss can now qualify for MDD diagnosis if criteria are met. This change raised concerns about pathologizing normal grief, illustrating medicalization concerns.

questions.q: According to the lecture, how did ancient civilizations explain mental illness through supernatural theories?
options: As a punishment from society for breaking moral codes
As the result of too much or too little blood flow to the brain
As possession by evil or demonic spirits, treated with exorcisms and witch-hunting
As purely psychological problems stemming from irrational thoughts
As genetic conditions inherited directly from ancestors
questions.explain: The notes state that supernatural theories, dominant in the Middle Ages and earlier, attributed odd behaviors to possession by evil or demonic spirits. Treatments included religious ceremonies, exorcisms, and witch-hunting, as well as trephination.

questions.q: What was trephination, and why was it performed according to supernatural theories?
options: Removing specific brain regions thought to control rational thought
Drilling holes in the skull to release evil spirits trapped within
A surgical procedure to balance the four humours in the body
A method to increase blood flow to improve mood
A technique to remove demonic possession by cutting the spine
questions.explain: The notes define trephination as drilling holes in the skull to release evil spirits, describing it as one of the oldest known surgical procedures. This illustrates how supernatural theories led to unusual medical treatments.

questions.q: Hippocrates' somatogenic theory attributed mental illness to imbalances in what?
options: Five essential body organs
Four essential bodily fluids: blood, yellow bile, black bile, and phlegm
Three primary hormonal systems
Six types of brain neurotransmitters
Seven different temperamental types
questions.explain: The notes specify that Hippocrates believed mental illness resulted from excess or deficiency of four bodily fluids: blood, yellow bile, black bile, and phlegm. This theory led to treatments like blood-letting.

questions.q: How did somatogenic theories attempt to treat mental illness, using an example from the lecture?
options: By encouraging religious prayer and spiritual reflection
By using psychological techniques to change irrational thoughts
By blood-letting for someone too temperamental (attributed to excess blood)
By prescribing cognitive behavioral therapy
By removing the patient from their social environment
questions.explain: The notes provide blood-letting as an example of somatogenic treatment—draining blood from someone perceived as having too much blood (the temperamental humour). This reflects the physical/bodily cause approach.

questions.q: Which of the following is a key development in psychogenic theories of mental illness?
options: The discovery that all mental illness has a genetic basis
The recognition that traumatic or stressful experiences and maladaptive cognitions contribute to mental illness
The invention of medication to control all psychiatric symptoms
The elimination of the need for any biological factors in diagnosis
The proof that mental illness is not related to learning or environment
questions.explain: The notes define psychogenic theories as attributing mental illness to traumatic or stressful experiences and maladaptive cognitions and behaviors. This led to treatments like psychoanalysis, behavioral therapy, and cognitive therapy.

questions.q: The biopsychosocial model represents a shift from earlier theories. Which statement BEST describes this model?
options: It focuses only on biological factors and ignores psychological and social influences
It attributes all mental illness solely to psychological trauma
It considers mental disorders as outcomes of interaction between biological, psychological, and social-cultural factors
It eliminates the need for psychological treatment in favor of medication
It argues that social factors are the only meaningful cause of mental illness
questions.explain: The notes state that the biopsychosocial approach, currently dominant, considers psychological disorders as outcomes of interaction between biological (genes, brain), psychological (stress, trauma, cognition), and social-cultural (norms, roles) factors.

questions.q: According to the biopsychosocial model, which domain includes factors like stress, trauma, and learned helplessness?
options: Biological factors
Psychological factors
Social-cultural factors
Neurological factors
Genetic factors
questions.explain: The model's table in the notes lists stress, trauma, learned helplessness, mood-related perceptions and memories under the Psychological domain. Biological includes genes and brain chemistry; social-cultural includes roles and definitions of disorder.

questions.q: What are risk factors for mental illness, and which of the following is NOT listed as an example in the lecture?
options: Genetics and substance use
Violence, poverty, and inequality
Strong social skills and positive relationships
Bullying and harsh parenting (especially during early childhood)
Economic downturns and humanitarian emergencies
questions.explain: Strong social skills and positive relationships are protective factors, not risk factors. The notes list substance use, genetics, poor emotional skills, poverty, violence, inequality, and other stressors as risk factors that increase likelihood of mental illness.

questions.q: Why are sensitive periods, particularly early childhood, important in understanding risk factors for mental illness?
options: Risks occurring during early childhood are no more harmful than risks in adulthood
Risks occurring during early childhood are particularly harmful to long-term mental health outcomes
Only biological risks matter; environmental risks during childhood have no effect
Children naturally recover from all adverse experiences without lasting effects
Mental illness cannot develop until adolescence, so childhood risks are irrelevant
questions.explain: The notes explicitly state that sensitive periods matter—risks occurring during early childhood are particularly harmful. Examples include bullying and harsh parenting, which can have lasting developmental impacts.

questions.q: Which of the following is a protective factor against mental illness, according to the lecture?
options: Social isolation and avoidance of relationships
Lack of access to education and employment
Safe neighborhoods, quality education, and community ties
Exposure to violence and economic instability
Weak social skills and poor communication
questions.explain: The notes list protective factors including social skills, positive social interactions, access to quality education, decent work, safe neighborhoods, and community ties. These factors reduce the likelihood or severity of mental disorders.

questions.q: According to the lecture, why is it inaccurate to attribute mental health outcomes to a single risk or protective factor?
options: Because mental illness is determined entirely by genetics
Because no risk factor is ever relevant to mental health
Because no single risk or protective factor can reliably and singlehandedly explain mental health outcomes—multiple factors interact
Because social factors are always more important than biological factors
Because mental health outcomes are entirely random and unpredictable
questions.explain: The notes explicitly state that no single risk or protective factor can reliably and singlehandedly explain mental health outcomes. This aligns with the biopsychosocial model's emphasis on interaction between multiple domains.

questions.q: The WHO's 2022 four-pillar framework for responding to the mental health crisis includes which of the following?
options: Only medication and hospitalization
Deepen value, Reshape environments, Strengthen care, and Value transformation
Punish those with mental illness to deter others
Replace community care with only institutional care
Eliminate all mental health diagnoses and treatment
questions.explain: The notes list the four WHO pillars: Deepen Value and Commitment, Reshape Environments, Strengthen Mental Health Care, and Value Transformation. Each pillar addresses different aspects of systemic mental health response.

questions.q: What does the WHO framework mean by 'Reshape Environments' as a response to the mental health crisis?
options: Only individual therapy should replace all other interventions
Modify physical, social, and economic characteristics of homes, schools, workplaces, and communities
Isolate people with mental illness from society
Increase use of medication without addressing social conditions
Eliminate all mental health services and rely only on self-help
questions.explain: The notes specify that 'Reshape Environments' means reshaping physical, social, and economic characteristics of homes, schools, workplaces, health care services, communities, and natural environments. This reflects the ecological perspective on mental health.

questions.q: According to the WHO framework, what change is recommended regarding psychiatric care models?
options: Expand custodial (institutional) care in psychiatric hospitals
Move away from custodial care toward community-based, rights-based models of care
Eliminate all mental health care services
Return to supernatural explanations for mental illness
Rely only on medication without psychological support
questions.explain: The notes explicitly state that the WHO framework calls for moving away from custodial (institutional) psychiatric care toward community-based, rights-based models. This reflects contemporary best practices in mental health treatment.

questions.q: Which of the following BEST illustrates how cultural context influences the definition of mental disorder?
options: All mental disorders are identical across all cultures worldwide
Koro and Hikikomori, while specific to certain regions initially, demonstrate how culture shapes symptom expression and recognition
Western definitions of mental illness are universally correct for all populations
Cultural differences in mental illness are purely semantic and have no real significance
Only developed Western countries have accurate definitions of mental disorder
questions.explain: The notes present Koro (Southeast Asia/Africa) and Hikikomori (Japan, later elsewhere) as examples of how culture shapes what symptoms are recognized as disorders and how they manifest. This shows cultural relativity in defining mental illness.

lectures.title: Lecture 4: Is There More to a Good Life Than Happiness?

questions.q: What does subjective well-being (SWB) measure?
options: The amount of money a person earns each year
An individual's thinking and feeling that their life is going well
A person's physical health status and fitness level
The number of close relationships someone maintains
A measure of intelligence and academic achievement
questions.explain: SWB is defined as the scientific concept for happiness — the thinking and feeling that one's life is going very well. It focuses on life satisfaction and subjective pleasure, not income, health status alone, or relational quantity. Answers A, C, and D confuse SWB with other constructs.

questions.q: Which of the following is NOT one of the three main components of subjective well-being?
options: Positive affect
Life satisfaction
Financial wealth
Negative affect
Emotional experience
questions.explain: SWB has three distinct components: positive affect (positive emotions), negative affect (negative emotions), and life satisfaction (overall judgment of life quality). Financial wealth is a separate variable that influences SWB but is not a component of it. This is a common exam trap.

questions.q: The Satisfaction with Life Scale (SWLS) measures well-being using how many items?
options: 3 items
5 items
7 items
10 items
15 items
questions.explain: The SWLS uses 5 items (closeness to ideal, excellent conditions, satisfaction, getting important things, would change nothing) on a 1–7 scale to assess global cognitive evaluation of life. The SPANE uses more items and the Cantril Ladder uses a 0–10 scale instead.

questions.q: According to research, happy people tend to exhibit all of the following EXCEPT:
options: Stronger immune systems and longer lifespans
More stable and rewarding relationships
Lower workplace productivity and earnings
More likely to donate to charitable causes
Better health behaviors like wearing seatbelts
questions.explain: Happy people are healthier, more sociable, more productive, and better citizens. Research shows that work units with higher SWB are more productive and companies with happy workers earn more money. Claiming lower productivity contradicts the evidence cited by Diener (2023).

questions.q: What does the broaden-and-build theory suggest about positive emotions?
options: They only last a few minutes before fading away
They widen thoughts and motivations, then spur development of enduring personal resources
They reduce the likelihood of future negative emotions
They increase a person's income and social status immediately
They are primarily useful during times of stress
questions.explain: Fredrickson's broaden-and-build theory has two distinct mechanisms: broadening widens thought repertoires and motivations (creativity, flexibility, openness); building spurs long-term development of resilience, social connection, and skills. This creates an upward spiral, not immediate income gains.

questions.q: The income–happiness relationship shows which pattern above a moderate income level (approximately US$10,000 per capita GDP)?
options: Happiness continues to increase at the same rapid rate
The relationship flattens; additional income produces only small increases in SWB
Income and happiness become negatively correlated
Happiness increases faster than at lower income levels
There is no relationship between income and happiness at all
questions.explain: Cross-national data show that life satisfaction rises steeply with GDP per capita at low incomes but flattens above ~US$10,000 (correlation = .08 above that level). Japan and the US exemplify this: despite large economic gains from 1958–2000, average life satisfaction remained constant.

questions.q: Which of the following best illustrates the hedonic adaptation phenomenon?
options: A person who inherits a large sum of money remains happier permanently
A person divorced or widowed experiences reduced happiness that gradually returns toward their original baseline level
A person's happiness increases linearly with each year of additional income
A person who moves to a happier country becomes permanently happier
A person's happiness depends primarily on their genes and cannot change
questions.explain: Adaptation (hedonic adaptation) means people react to life events but reactions dampen over time, with SWB returning toward its baseline level. Evidence from the German Panel Study (n=24,000) shows this for widowhood, divorce, unemployment, and marriage — though the extent of adaptation varies.

questions.q: The valuing happiness paradox (Mauss et al., 2011) suggests that:
options: Happy people always live in low-stress environments
Pursuing happiness directly often increases happiness regardless of life stress
Under low life stress, those who valued happiness more were less happy and more depressed
Happiness can only be achieved by not thinking about it
People who value happiness are more successful financially
questions.explain: Mauss et al. (2011) found that among people with low life stress, those who valued happiness more were less happy, less satisfied, less flourishing, and reported more depression symptoms. This counterintuitive result shows that maximizing happiness as a goal can undermine the experience itself.

questions.q: Construal theory of happiness suggests that objective circumstances affect happiness through which psychological processes?
options: Only genetic inheritance and early childhood experiences
Social comparison, savoring, and gratitude
Income level and geographic location alone
Physical exercise and dietary choices exclusively
Age and marital status primarily
questions.explain: Lyubomirsky's construal theory (2001) explains that objective circumstances affect happiness through multiple psychological processes including social comparison, savoring, and gratitude — not just external factors like income or location.

questions.q: Which intervention showed that participants who wrote weekly gratitude journals for 10 weeks reported:
options: Increased social media usage and more online friendships
Better life satisfaction and fewer physical symptoms compared to control groups
No significant change in well-being or health outcomes
Higher income levels and career advancement
Decreased negative affect but unchanged life satisfaction
questions.explain: Emmons et al. (2003) demonstrated that gratitude journal participants (vs. hassles or neutral events) reported better life satisfaction and fewer physical symptoms. This is a concrete intervention supporting the construal theory mechanism.

questions.q: The prosocial spending experiment (Dunn et al., 2008) found that participants who received money to spend on others reported:
options: The same happiness levels as those who spent on themselves
Lower happiness due to guilt about giving
Higher subsequent happiness compared to those who spent on themselves
Increased financial anxiety and concern about the recipient
Temporary happiness that faded within hours
questions.explain: Dunn et al. (2008) showed that participants given money to spend on others (donations or gifts) reported higher subsequent happiness than those who spent on themselves. This demonstrates the happiness-boosting effect of prosocial behavior.

questions.q: According to recent research, which environmental factor is consistently associated with better subjective well-being?
options: Urban living and high population density
Frequent visits to green spaces and blue spaces, plus nature connectedness
Living in a tropical climate year-round
Distance from natural water bodies
Reduced exposure to sunlight and outdoor activities
questions.explain: White et al. (2021) found that frequency of visits to green and blue spaces, and general nature connectedness, were positively associated with positive well-being across 18 countries. A Hong Kong study (Ma et al., 2025) with 2,800+ students confirmed stronger nature connectedness predicted lower likelihood of poor well-being.

questions.q: Heavy use of social media, internet, and gaming is associated with which pattern of well-being?
options: Increased subjective well-being across all demographic groups
Lower happiness, potentially due to displacement, upward social comparison, and cyberbullying
No significant relationship with happiness or well-being
Increased well-being in adolescents but decreased well-being in adults
Higher life satisfaction in girls but lower in boys
questions.explain: Twenge & Farley (2021) found that heavy digital media use is associated with lower happiness in both girls and boys. Proposed mechanisms include displacement of beneficial activities, upward social comparison, and cyberbullying.

questions.q: How does the happiness-maximization ideal differ across cultures?
options: All cultures equally prioritize happiness as the core of a good life
Happiness maximization is a WEIRD phenomenon; ideal happiness levels vary enormously across countries
Non-Western cultures always value happiness less than Western cultures
Eastern cultures uniformly reject the concept of happiness entirely
The concept of happiness is identical in all human societies
questions.explain: Krys et al. (2024) show that happiness maximization emerged particularly in Northwestern European cultures. Cross-national data reveal huge variation in how high people want their happiness to be — it is not a universal ideal.

questions.q: According to the lecture, which of the following is NOT mentioned as a cultural component of a good life?
options: Harmony with relationships and nature
Meaning and purpose
Spirituality and religiosity
Subjective well-being and life satisfaction
Social media influence and online status
questions.explain: The lecture identifies subjective well-being, meaning, harmony, and spirituality as key cultural components of a good life across different cultures. Social media influence and online status are not presented as traditional cultural ideals of a good life.

questions.q: Eudaimonic well-being, as described by Ryff, includes all of the following components EXCEPT:
options: Self-acceptance and positive relationships
Autonomy and environmental mastery
Purpose in life and personal growth
Maximum accumulation of wealth and possessions
Sense of competence in managing one's environment
questions.explain: Ryff's six components of eudaimonic well-being are: self-acceptance, positive relationships, autonomy, environmental mastery, purpose in life, and personal growth. Wealth accumulation is not a component; eudaimonic well-being focuses on meaning and virtue, not material possessions.

questions.q: What is the key distinction between hedonic and eudaimonic well-being?
options: Hedonic well-being is about pleasure and happiness; eudaimonic is about meaning, virtue, and flourishing
Eudaimonic well-being is the same as hedonic well-being, just a different term
Hedonic well-being requires more time and effort than eudaimonic well-being
Eudaimonic well-being only applies to wealthy individuals
Both concepts are equally emphasized in Western cultures
questions.explain: Hedonic well-being = pleasure and happiness. Eudaimonic well-being (Aristotle's concept) = doing what is worth doing, pursuing meaning and virtue. A person can be eudaimonically well (pursuing meaningful goals) while experiencing low hedonic pleasure — they are distinct constructs.

questions.q: Why might a person pursuing important life goals experience high eudaimonic well-being but low hedonic pleasure?
options: Pursuing goals always increases both types of well-being equally
Meaningful activities do not necessarily produce immediate pleasure, but contribute to purpose and flourishing
Eudaimonic well-being is impossible without also experiencing high pleasure
This situation is a psychological contradiction that cannot occur
Goals and pleasure are unrelated to well-being
questions.explain: Not all meaningful activities produce hedonic pleasure. A person struggling through medical school, raising a difficult child, or fighting for justice may experience low immediate pleasure but high purpose and meaning — high eudaimonic but low hedonic well-being.

questions.q: The research on income and happiness from Japan and the United States demonstrates:
options: Income increases always lead to proportional increases in happiness
Despite large economic prosperity growth (1958–2000), average life satisfaction remained remarkably constant
Wealthier nations have uniformly happier populations than poorer nations
The relationship between income and happiness strengthens over time
Economic growth guarantees increased happiness for all citizens
questions.explain: Despite substantial increases in economic prosperity from 1958–2000 in both Japan and the US, average life satisfaction stayed remarkably constant (Diener & Seligman, 2004). This demonstrates the income–happiness relationship flattens at higher income levels.

questions.q: Which mechanism is NOT proposed to explain the relationship between heavy digital media use and lower happiness?
options: Displacement of beneficial offline activities like exercise and social connection
Upward social comparison with others' idealized online presentations
Cyberbullying and online harassment
Increased time outdoors and nature exposure
Reduction in face-to-face social interaction quality
questions.explain: Proposed mechanisms linking heavy digital media use to lower happiness are: displacement of beneficial activities, upward social comparison, and cyberbullying. Increased outdoor time and nature exposure would be the opposite mechanism — it would increase happiness.

questions.q: According to the broaden-and-build theory, how do positive emotions contribute to lasting health benefits?
options: They eliminate negative emotions permanently
They broaden thought patterns immediately, then build lasting resources over time, creating an upward spiral
They increase income directly
They are only effective for people without stress
They provide temporary comfort without long-term effects
questions.explain: The broaden-and-build theory shows that positive emotions widen thoughts (broaden hypothesis), which spurs development of enduring resources like resilience and skills (build hypothesis), creating an upward spiral that enhances health, survival, and fulfillment.

questions.q: The research on pro-environmental behavior and subjective well-being (Prinzing, 2024) found that:
options: Environmental activities always decrease happiness due to stress
Participants doing three good things for the planet reported better SWB the next day compared to controls
Environmental behavior has no effect on happiness levels
Only fun activities increase well-being, not environmental actions
Environmental awareness is negatively correlated with life satisfaction
questions.explain: Prinzing (2024) showed that participants instructed to do three good things for the planet reported better SWB the next day compared to control conditions. Interestingly, the fun condition showed similar gains, suggesting both meaningful and enjoyable activities boost well-being.

questions.q: Which of the following best summarizes why happiness alone may be insufficient as a measure of a good life?
options: Happiness is the only valid indicator of well-being across all cultures
A good life involves meaning, purpose, harmony, and virtue — not just pleasant feelings
Measures of happiness are always scientifically inaccurate
Cultural variation in values does not affect what constitutes a good life
Eudaimonic well-being is less important than hedonic pleasure in all contexts
questions.explain: The lecture challenges the reduction of a good life to happiness alone by introducing eudaimonic well-being and showing that cultural variation, the paradox of valuing happiness, and the complexity of human goals suggest a good life involves more than hedonic pleasure.

questions.q: What is the primary source of variation in 'ideal happiness levels' across different countries?
options: Geographic latitude and climate conditions
Economic development level determines all happiness ideals universally
Cultural values and different philosophies about what constitutes a good life
Average lifespan and health outcomes in each nation
Population density and urbanization rates
questions.explain: Krys et al. (2024) demonstrate that the perceived ideal level of happiness varies enormously across countries due to different cultural values and philosophies. The WEIRD phenomenon shows happiness maximization is not universal but culturally specific.

questions.q: In East Asian and collectivist cultures, which component of a good life is particularly emphasized?
options: Individual happiness maximization above all else
Harmony with others and with nature
Spiritual rebellion against social norms
Accumulation of personal wealth
Competitive achievement and status
questions.explain: According to Krys et al. (2024), East Asian and collectivist cultures particularly emphasize harmony (relationship harmony and harmony with nature) as a key component of a good life, not individual happiness maximization.

questions.q: How many components make up Ryff's model of eudaimonic well-being?
options: Three components
Four components
Six components
Eight components
Twelve components
questions.explain: Ryff's model identifies six components of eudaimonic well-being: self-acceptance, positive relationships, autonomy, environmental mastery, purpose in life, and personal growth. These form a comprehensive framework for flourishing beyond hedonic pleasure.

questions.q: All of the following are main causes of happiness according to Diener EXCEPT:
options: Income, particularly at lower levels
Cognitive processes like social comparison and gratitude
Life events and how we adapt to them
Behavioral choices like volunteering and prosocial spending
Genetic predisposition making change impossible
questions.explain: Diener identifies four main clusters: income (especially at low levels), life events (with adaptation dampening effects), cognitive construal processes, and behavioral choices. The lecture emphasizes that happiness is not purely genetically determined — thoughts and actions matter significantly.

questions.q: What correlation coefficient is reported for the income–happiness relationship above approximately US$10,000 per capita GDP?
options: Negative correlation of -0.15
questions.explain: Diener & Seligman (2004) found a correlation of .08 between income and happiness above the US$10,000 per capita GDP threshold, indicating a very weak relationship at higher income levels despite the strong relationship at lower income levels.

questions.q: The difference between life satisfaction and positive/negative affect is important because:
options: They are the same concept with different names
A person can have high positive affect but low life satisfaction, showing they are distinct components
Life satisfaction is the only component that matters for SWB
Positive and negative affect are not part of SWB at all
Affect and satisfaction are correlated so perfectly they measure identical concepts
questions.explain: A key exam trap is conflating SWB's three components. A person can have frequent pleasant emotions (high positive affect) yet feel dissatisfied with their life overall (low life satisfaction), or vice versa. These are distinct and must not be conflated.

questions.q: According to the lecture, spirituality and religiosity are emphasized as components of a good life in which cultural contexts?
options: Primarily in Western, Educated, Industrialized, Rich, Democratic (WEIRD) societies
Only in wealthy developed nations
Many non-Western cultures, where they are valued alongside happiness and meaning
Exclusively in East Asian collectivist cultures
They are equally emphasized across all cultures worldwide
questions.explain: The lecture notes that spirituality and religiosity are key elements of a good life in many non-Western cultures, contrasting with the Western happiness-maximization ideal. Krys et al. (2024) demonstrates that different cultures emphasize different components — happiness is just one element, not universal.

lectures.title: Lecture 5: What Do Most People Get Wrong About Schizophrenia?

questions.q: According to WHO 2025, what is the global prevalence rate of anxiety disorders?
questions.explain: The lecture specifies WHO 2025 global prevalence for anxiety disorders as 4.4%. The incorrect options are either half this rate (2.2%), double (8.8%), or other plausible distractors. Students must recall the exact statistic.

questions.q: Which of the following best defines the core distinction between 'free-floating anxiety' and anxiety tied to a specific trigger?
options: Free-floating anxiety has no particular object of worry; triggered anxiety focuses on a specific, identifiable threat
Free-floating anxiety is more dangerous than triggered anxiety
Free-floating anxiety only occurs in the morning
Free-floating anxiety lasts longer than triggered anxiety
Free-floating anxiety involves physical symptoms while triggered anxiety is purely psychological
questions.explain: GAD is characterized by 'free-floating anxiety' — worry not tied to a specific trigger — as opposed to phobias or panic attacks tied to identifiable stimuli. The other options misrepresent the definition or confuse severity with duration.
