questions.q: A patient experiences an intense, sudden fear of spiders triggered by seeing one in their home. This fear leads them to avoid the basement entirely. Which anxiety disorder classification best fits this presentation?
options: Generalized Anxiety Disorder
Panic Disorder
Phobia
Agoraphobia
Panic Disorder with Agoraphobia
questions.explain: The clinical presentation — specific fear trigger (spider), avoidance behavior, and fear out of proportion to actual threat — defines a phobia (animal type). GAD lacks a specific trigger; panic disorder involves unexpected attacks unrelated to specific objects; agoraphobia concerns escape difficulty, not animal fear.

questions.q: Which of the following is classified as a subtype of phobia according to the lecture?
options: Generalized worry about family finances
Intense fear of riding in elevators
Unexpected panic attacks throughout the day
Obsessive thoughts about contamination
Belief that others are plotting against you
questions.explain: Elevators are a situational phobia. Generalized worry defines GAD; unexpected panic attacks define panic disorder; obsessive thoughts define OCD; suspicious beliefs define paranoid personality disorder. Only the elevator fear matches the phobia category.

questions.q: What is the core difference between a panic attack and panic disorder?
options: A panic attack is a single episode; panic disorder is multiple episodes across different situations
A panic attack involves chest pain; panic disorder involves only psychological symptoms
A panic attack is always triggered by a specific situation; panic disorder is unprovoked
A panic attack lasts hours; panic disorder lasts days
A panic attack requires medical intervention; panic disorder does not
questions.explain: The exam trap in the notes clarifies: a panic attack alone does not equal panic disorder. Panic disorder requires unexpected, recurring attacks across situations without a specific trigger. A single panic attack is not diagnostic of the disorder.

questions.q: During a panic attack, a patient reports feeling as though they are about to die. Which physiological symptom commonly accompanies this fear in panic disorder?
options: Hypothermia and shivering
Slowed heart rate and low blood pressure
Racing heart rate and chest pain
Muscle relaxation and drowsiness
Hypersalivation and nausea only
questions.explain: Racing heart rate and chest pain are core physiological panic symptoms listed in the lecture. The other options represent either opposite effects (slowed heart rate, muscle relaxation) or incomplete symptom profiles. Students must recognize the cardinal physical panic markers.

questions.q: According to the cognitive perspective, what is the maladaptive thought pattern characteristic of anxiety disorders?
options: Difficulty concentrating on tasks
Catastrophizing — predicting terrible outcomes despite contrary evidence
Excessive daydreaming about positive future events
Inability to recall recent memories
Overconfidence in dangerous situations
questions.explain: The lecture cites catastrophizing as the key cognitive distortion in anxiety — anxious people tend to predict terrible outcomes despite contrary evidence. The other options either describe symptoms of other conditions or represent the opposite cognitive bias (overconfidence).

questions.q: In the behavioral perspective, how are phobias acquired and then maintained according to classical and operant conditioning principles?
options: Acquisition through observational learning; maintenance through punishment
Acquisition through classical conditioning; maintenance through negative reinforcement (avoidance reducing anxiety)
Acquisition through operant conditioning only; maintenance through positive reinforcement
Acquisition through cognitive distortion; maintenance through social modeling
Acquisition through genetic predisposition only; maintenance through environmental stress
questions.explain: The lecture explicitly links classical conditioning (acquisition) and operant conditioning via negative reinforcement (maintenance via avoidance). When avoidance reduces anxiety, the phobic response is reinforced, perpetuating the disorder. The other options misapply learning principles.

questions.q: What is the distinguishing feature of Major Depressive Disorder compared to normal sadness?
options: Depressed mood only in the afternoon
Depressed mood that persists most of the day, nearly every day, for at least two weeks
Depressed mood that lasts only a few hours
Depressed mood triggered exclusively by external loss
Depressed mood accompanied by hallucinations only
questions.explain: MDD requires persistent depressed mood most of the day, nearly every day, for at least two weeks — a criterion that distinguishes it from normal mood fluctuations. The other options misrepresent the duration or trigger pattern of depression.

questions.q: How do the global prevalence rates of Major Depressive Disorder and Anxiety Disorders compare?
options: MDD is twice as common as anxiety disorders
Anxiety disorders are slightly more common than MDD
MDD and anxiety disorders have identical prevalence rates
Anxiety disorders are rare; MDD is the most common mental disorder
Neither has been measured by WHO 2025
questions.explain: The lecture specifies MDD global prevalence as 4% overall and 5.7% for adults, while anxiety disorders are 4.4% — roughly comparable but anxiety slightly higher. The option correctly identifies this near-parity with slight anxiety predominance.

questions.q: What is the key difference between Type I and Type II Bipolar Disorder?
options: Type I is more common than Type II
Type I involves mania; Type II involves hypomania, not full mania
Type I has only depressive episodes
Type II is a less severe form of anxiety disorder
Type I only affects women; Type II only affects men
questions.explain: The lecture and exam trap clarify: Type I includes one or more manic episodes; Type II includes only hypomanic episodes plus depression, but no full manic episode. This is a high-yield distinction students commonly confuse. The other options are factually incorrect.

questions.q: During a manic episode in bipolar disorder, which of the following cognitive symptoms is characteristic?
options: Slowness of thought and obsessive worrying
Racing thoughts, flight of ideas, and delusions of grandeur
Loss of memory for recent events
Inability to form any thoughts
Paranoid delusions about government surveillance
questions.explain: The lecture's comparison table lists racing thoughts, flight of ideas, and delusions of grandeur as manic cognitive features. The first option describes depressive cognition; the others misrepresent manic or other psychotic presentations.

questions.q: Which motor and behavioral symptom distinguishes a manic episode from a depressive episode in bipolar disorder?
options: Both involve decreased sleep but opposite activity levels
Manic: hyperactive and less sleep; Depressive: less active and difficulty sleeping
Manic: less active and more sleep; Depressive: hyperactive and less sleep
Both involve identical motor symptoms but opposite mood
Motor symptoms are irrelevant to the manic-depressive distinction
questions.explain: The table contrasts manic hyperactivity/less sleep with depressive low activity/sleep difficulty. While both episodes disrupt sleep, their motor profiles are opposite — hyperactivity vs. inactivity. Students must distinguish the motor signatures of each episode type.

questions.q: According to Beck's cognitive model of depression, what is the sequence from early experience to depressive episode?
options: Depressive episode → stressful event → negative schemas → adverse experiences
Adverse experiences → dysfunctional attitudes and negative schemas → stressful event activates schemas → depression
Stressful event → temporary sadness → depression without schema involvement
Negative thoughts → genetic predisposition → depression
Environmental stress only; early experiences have no role
questions.explain: Beck's model (cited in the lecture) follows a developmental sequence: adverse early experiences create dysfunctional attitudes and negative schemas; later stressful events activate these schemas, triggering depression. The other options either reverse the sequence or omit key stages.

questions.q: Which statement about schizophrenia prevalence is accurate according to the lecture?
options: Schizophrenia is the most common mental disorder worldwide
Schizophrenia affects approximately 0.29% of the global population overall and 0.43% of adults
Schizophrenia is more common than bipolar disorder
Schizophrenia affects less than 0.1% of the population
Schizophrenia prevalence has increased since 2020
questions.explain: The lecture specifies: global prevalence 0.29% overall; 0.43% among adults. These exact figures distinguish it from other disorders and highlight its lower-than-expected prevalence despite media prominence. The other options either overstate prevalence or provide incorrect statistics.

questions.q: Why is the common public perception that schizophrenia equals 'split personality' a critical misconception?
options: Split personality is a synonym for schizophrenia and the terms are interchangeable
Split personality (dissociative identity disorder) is a separate condition entirely; schizophrenia's 'split' refers to a split from reality, not identity
Both conditions are identical but called by different names in different countries
Schizophrenia is more serious than split personality
Split personality occurs only in schizophrenia
questions.explain: The lecture emphasizes this as the most widespread public misconception: schizophrenia is not dissociative identity disorder. The 'split' in schizophrenia means disconnection from reality (hallucinations, delusions), not fragmented identity. This distinction is critical for exam success.

questions.q: Which of the following is NOT listed as a core symptom of schizophrenia according to the lecture?
options: Persistent delusions and hallucinations
Obsessive thoughts about symmetry and order
Disorganized thinking manifested as jumbled speech
Negative symptoms including limited speech and emotional restriction
Catatonic symptoms such as extreme agitation or movement slowing
questions.explain: Obsessive thoughts about symmetry define OCD, not schizophrenia. The lecture lists delusions, hallucinations, disorganized thinking/behavior, negative symptoms, and catatonic symptoms as core schizophrenia features. This 'which is NOT' question tests whether students can distinguish schizophrenia from OCD.

questions.q: What does the dopamine hypothesis propose about the neurobiological basis of schizophrenia?
options: Schizophrenia results from too little dopamine activity in the brain
Schizophrenia results from excess dopamine activity; dopamine-blocking drugs effectively reduce symptoms
Dopamine has no role in schizophrenia; only serotonin is involved
Schizophrenia is purely genetic and dopamine is irrelevant
Dopamine blockade worsens schizophrenia symptoms
questions.explain: The dopamine hypothesis proposes excess dopamine activity in schizophrenia; dopamine-blocking antipsychotics effectively reduce symptoms. The lecture cites this as a major causal mechanism. The other options either reverse the hypothesis or incorrectly state drug effects.

questions.q: According to the diathesis-stress model presented in the lecture, which two factors jointly produce schizophrenia onset?
options: Only genetic factors; environmental factors play no role
Only environmental stressors; genetics are irrelevant
Genetic vulnerability and environmental stressors as triggers; early signs may appear before full onset
Family dysfunction alone, independent of genetics
Neurotransmitter imbalance without any genetic component
questions.explain: The diathesis-stress model integrates genetic predisposition with environmental triggers; early vulnerability signs (social withdrawal, movement abnormalities) can appear well before full disorder onset. This interactionist model rejects both pure-nature and pure-nurture explanations.

questions.q: What is the approximate lifetime risk of schizophrenia for the identical twin of a person with schizophrenia?
questions.explain: The lecture's genetic risk table lists ~48% lifetime risk for identical twins — the highest among all relationships, supporting the strong genetic basis. This figure is crucial for understanding schizophrenia's heritability. The other percentages represent lower-risk relationships (siblings, fraternal twins, or general population).

questions.q: How does the lifetime schizophrenia risk for a child of one schizophrenic parent compare to a child of two schizophrenic parents?
options: One parent: ~13%; two parents: ~46% (risk increases with number of affected parents)
One parent: ~46%; two parents: ~13% (counterintuitively lower with both parents)
Both carry identical ~20% risk regardless of parent count
One parent: ~1%; two parents: ~9% (environmental factor dominates)
Parental status is irrelevant to offspring risk
questions.explain: The lecture's table shows ~13% risk for one affected parent and ~46% for two — a clear dose-response illustrating genetic transmission. The gradient of risk (one parent vs. two parents vs. siblings vs. fraternal twins vs. general population) is a high-yield memorization point.

questions.q: What distinguishes obsessions from compulsions in Obsessive-Compulsive Disorder?
options: Obsessions are compulsions performed in secret; compulsions are public
Obsessions are repetitive thoughts; compulsions are repetitive behaviors or mental acts designed to reduce anxiety from obsessions
Obsessions are enjoyable while compulsions cause distress
Obsessions and compulsions are the same thing with different labels
Obsessions always involve contamination fear; compulsions do not
questions.explain: The lecture defines obsessions as repetitive, intrusive thoughts and compulsions as ritualized behaviors or mental acts performed to reduce the anxiety those obsessions cause. The exam trap notes compulsions are performed to reduce anxiety, not for pleasure. This thought-action relationship is fundamental.

questions.q: A patient with OCD experiences obsessive thoughts about having left the stove on. Which compulsive behavior would be consistent with this obsession?
options: Repeated handwashing rituals
Repeatedly checking the stove to verify it is off
Engaging in aggressive thoughts
Arranging objects symmetrically
Counting in specific patterns
questions.explain: The lecture's obsession-compulsion table links fear of contamination to washing, aggressive thoughts to checking, and ordering concerns to arranging. Stove-checking obsessions logically pair with checking compulsions. Students must match obsessive themes to appropriate compulsions.

questions.q: Body dysmorphic disorder and hoarding disorder are classified under OCD-related disorders. What do they share with OCD?
options: All three involve repetitive thoughts and behaviors
All three involve preoccupation with appearance defects only
All three manifest as fears of contamination
All three require hospitalization
Body dysmorphic disorder and hoarding are unrelated to OCD
questions.explain: Body dysmorphic disorder (preoccupation with perceived defects) and hoarding disorder (difficulty discarding possessions) are OCD-related because they share the core feature of repetitive thoughts and/or behaviors. The other options either mischaracterize these conditions or overstate severity.

questions.q: Personality disorders differ from other mental disorders in a fundamental way. Which statement best captures this distinction?
options: Personality disorders develop suddenly in adulthood, while other disorders develop gradually from childhood
Personality disorders are personality styles that are rigid, inflexible, and cause interpersonal conflict, whereas other disorders may be more episodic or situational
Personality disorders are purely genetic, while other disorders are purely environmental
Personality disorders have no neurobiological basis
Personality disorders are less serious than anxiety or mood disorders
questions.explain: The lecture defines personality disorders as personality styles that deviate from social norms, are rigid/inflexible, and create interpersonal barriers — a distinct pattern from episodic disorders like anxiety or mood disorders. This characterization emphasizes chronicity and relational dysfunction.

questions.q: What is the key distinguishing feature of paranoid personality disorder that prevents it from being classified as a psychotic disorder?
options: Paranoid personality disorder involves fixed delusions and hallucinations like schizophrenia
Paranoid personality disorder involves pervasive mistrust without psychotic features such as delusions or hallucinations
Paranoid personality disorder is more severe than schizophrenia
Paranoid personality disorder has a higher prevalence than schizophrenia
The lecture does not address this distinction
questions.explain: The exam trap explicitly notes: paranoid personality disorder is NOT schizophrenia or psychotic disorder. It involves mistrust and suspicion without delusions or hallucinations — the absence of these psychotic features is what prevents its classification as a psychotic disorder.

questions.q: Which personality disorder is characterized by continuous violation of others' rights, lack of empathy, and irresponsibility, with antisocial behavior required before age 15?
options: Paranoid personality disorder
Narcissistic personality disorder
Borderline personality disorder
Antisocial personality disorder
Obsessive-compulsive personality disorder
questions.explain: The table lists antisocial PD features: rights violations, historical antisocial behavior predating age 15, deceitfulness, impulsivity, lack of empathy and remorse, irresponsibility. The age-15 requirement is a key diagnostic criterion distinguishing antisocial PD from other personality disorders.

questions.q: A person with borderline personality disorder seeks constant reassurance from friends, experiences intense anger when alone, and reports chronic feelings of emptiness. Which feature best explains their relationship instability?
options: Excessive confidence in others
Inability to tolerate being alone combined with unstable relationships and impulsivity
Rational detachment from emotions
Excessive planning and rigidity
High empathy leading to overinvolvement
questions.explain: Borderline PD involves unstable self-image, inability to tolerate aloneness, chronic emptiness, and unstable/intense relationships — this combination creates relational turbulence. The exam must recognize this distinctive profile. The other options describe either opposite traits or other personality disorders.

questions.q: According to the WHO 2025 prevalence data presented in the lecture, which mental disorder has the highest global prevalence rate?
options: Schizophrenia at 0.3%
Bipolar disorder at 0.5%
Anxiety disorders at 4.4%
Autism spectrum disorders at 0.8%
OCD and related disorders at 1.1%
questions.explain: The lecture's prevalence table shows anxiety disorders at 4.4% as the highest rate, followed by depression at 4%. Schizophrenia at 0.3% has the second-lowest prevalence despite media prominence. Students must retain these comparative prevalence figures for exam success.

questions.q: What does the lecture emphasize about schizophrenia's actual prevalence compared to its media representation?
options: Schizophrenia is the most common mental disorder, justifying extensive media coverage
Despite high media prominence, schizophrenia has the second-lowest prevalence (0.3%) among major disorders
Media rarely mentions schizophrenia because it is so rare
Schizophrenia prevalence has decreased due to media awareness campaigns
Prevalence data are unreliable for schizophrenia
questions.explain: The lecture explicitly notes this paradox: schizophrenia, despite media prominence and historical stigma, has the second-lowest prevalence (0.3%) — lower than anxiety (4.4%), depression (4%), OCD (1.1%), and autism (0.8%). This mismatch is a key learning point highlighting misconceptions.

lectures.title: Lecture 6: What Exactly Happens During Psychotherapy?

questions.q: Which of the following is NOT considered a psychotropic medication?
options: Antipsychotics
Antidepressants
Antihistamines
Mood stabilizers
Antianxiety agents
questions.explain: Psychotropic medications include antipsychotics, antidepressants, antianxiety agents, and mood stabilizers. Antihistamines are not psychotropic medications — they treat allergies and other non-psychiatric conditions. The exam trap is assuming all psychiatric drugs are psychotropic.

questions.q: What is the primary difference between psychotropic medications and psychotherapy as treatments?
options: Medications treat disorders while psychotherapy treats problems in living
Medications are cheaper than psychotherapy
Medications affect brain chemistry while psychotherapy uses psychological techniques
Medications work faster than psychotherapy
Medications have no side effects while psychotherapy does
questions.explain: Psychotropic medications operate through chemical/biological mechanisms affecting neurotransmitters and brain function, whereas psychotherapy uses psychological techniques including learning, cognition, and behaviour modification. Both can treat disorders or address problems in living; the distinction is the mechanism, not the target.

questions.q: In systematic desensitization, what is the role of relaxation training?
options: It is used to replace the feared stimulus entirely
It prevents the client from experiencing any anxiety
It allows the client to tolerate gradually higher levels of the feared stimulus
It trains clients to avoid the feared stimulus indefinitely
It eliminates the anxiety hierarchy
questions.explain: Relaxation training in systematic desensitization enables counterconditioning — the client learns to pair relaxation with gradually increasing exposure to the feared stimulus, moving up the anxiety hierarchy. Relaxation does not eliminate fear entirely or replace exposure; rather, it enables tolerance of progressively stronger feared stimuli.

questions.q: Which exposure method is used in systematic desensitization for dog phobia: first observing from 100 feet, then 50 feet, then 25 feet?
options: In vivo exposure with relaxation
Imagined exposure with relaxation
Response prevention without relaxation
Aversion therapy
Participant modeling
questions.explain: In vivo (in real life) exposure to the actual feared object (the dog) at increasing distances is paired with relaxation training. This is distinct from imagined exposure (visualizing the feared stimulus) and from response prevention (blocking compulsive responses).

questions.q: What is the key mechanism that distinguishes exposure therapy from systematic desensitization?
options: Exposure therapy uses imagined stimuli while desensitization uses real stimuli
Exposure therapy omits relaxation training and relies on extinction of the fear response
Exposure therapy is faster because it uses more intense stimuli
Exposure therapy is only for phobias while desensitization treats all anxiety
Exposure therapy requires a therapist to model the feared situation
questions.explain: Exposure therapy deliberately omits relaxation training and aims for extinction of the fear or avoidance response through direct confrontation with the feared stimulus. In contrast, systematic desensitization pairs relaxation with gradual exposure. The exam trap is confusing these two mechanisms.

questions.q: In exposure therapy for OCD (obsessive-compulsive disorder), what does 'response prevention' mean?
options: The therapist prevents the client from entering anxiety-provoking situations
The client is taught to prevent anxious thoughts from entering consciousness
The compulsive response (e.g., handwashing) is blocked or prevented
The client practices preventing exposure to feared stimuli
The avoidance response is prevented through flooding
questions.explain: Response prevention in exposure therapy specifically blocks the compulsive response — for example, preventing an OCD patient from washing their hands after exposure to contamination concerns. This allows extinction of both the compulsion and the underlying anxiety. Blocking avoidance is distinct from blocking compulsion.

questions.q: Which behavioural technique pairs an unwanted behaviour with an unpleasant stimulus to reduce it?
options: Token economy
Fearless peer
Aversion therapy
Participant modeling
Systematic desensitization
questions.explain: Aversion therapy deliberately pairs an unwanted behaviour with an unpleasant stimulus so the client learns to avoid the behaviour. Token economy rewards desired behaviours; fearless peer uses modelling; participant modeling involves therapist guidance; systematic desensitization uses relaxation, not aversion.

questions.q: What is the primary goal of cognitive approaches to therapy?
options: Replace maladaptive behaviours with adaptive ones through reinforcement
Release unconscious conflicts from childhood
Replace irrational thoughts with more rational, adaptive thoughts
Create a supportive environment without challenging the client's beliefs
Expose clients to feared stimuli until anxiety extinguishes
questions.explain: Cognitive approaches aim to change the client's thinking through cognitive restructuring (reappraisal), replacing irrational or dysfunctional thoughts with more rational, adaptive ones. The core assumption is that negative emotions stem from irrational thinking. Behaviour change is secondary in pure cognitive therapy, though it may occur in cognitive-behavioural therapy.

questions.q: In the confrontational style of cognitive restructuring, what is the therapist's primary role?
options: To guide the client to discover disconfirming evidence themselves
To directly challenge and attack dysfunctional beliefs
To remain neutral and non-directive
To model the feared situation
To teach relaxation techniques
questions.explain: The confrontational style involves the therapist directly challenging dysfunctional beliefs (e.g., 'knock that out of your head'). The Socratic/teacher-guided style, by contrast, guides the client to gather disconfirming evidence themselves through questioning and homework.

questions.q: What distinguishes the Socratic style from the confrontational style in cognitive therapy?
options: Socratic style is slower and less effective
Socratic style guides the client to discover disconfirming evidence rather than being told it directly
Socratic style uses more intense challenges
Socratic style only works for depression
Socratic style omits homework assignments
questions.explain: In Socratic/teacher-guided cognitive restructuring, the therapist asks questions and assigns homework to help the client discover disconfirming evidence on their own (e.g., testing whether 'my husband doesn't love me'). The confrontational style directly attacks beliefs without this discovery process. Both are valid approaches with different stylistic emphasis.

questions.q: What does cognitive bias modification (CBM) attempt to change?
options: The conscious thoughts and beliefs the client verbally expresses
The client's core personality traits and values
Automatic attentional and interpretive biases through repeated practice
The client's past memories and unconscious conflicts
The neurochemistry of the brain through medication
questions.explain: CBM targets maladaptive automatic cognitive and attentional styles (e.g., focusing on the one distracted face in a crowd for socially anxious people) through systematic, repeated practice of an alternative style. It goes beyond conscious thought change and produces measurable physiological effects (e.g., lower cortisol levels).

questions.q: In the Dandeneau et al. (2007) study on CBM, what was the outcome of training participants to search for smiling faces?
options: Participants became more anxious in social situations
Participants showed reduced work stress and lower cortisol levels
Participants developed a dependency on the training app
Participants were unable to attend to other visual information
Participants showed no difference compared to controls
questions.explain: Training participants to search for smiling faces (positive stimuli) instead of flowers reduced their rated work stress and led to measurably lower cortisol levels compared to controls. This demonstrates that CBM produces real physiological and emotional benefits through repeated practice of an alternative attentional style.

questions.q: Which psychoanalytic technique involves the client freely voicing whatever comes to mind without censorship?
options: Participant modeling
Dream analysis
Free association
Systematic desensitization
Token economy
questions.explain: Free association is a core psychoanalytic technique where clients speak without filtering their thoughts, allowing unconscious material to emerge. Dream analysis interprets symbolic content of dreams. These are foundational techniques in psychoanalytic therapy aimed at releasing hidden unconscious impulses and conflicts.

questions.q: What is the primary therapeutic goal of psychoanalytic therapy?
options: To teach relaxation and exposure techniques
To replace irrational thoughts with rational ones
To release hidden unconscious impulses, conflicts, and memories
To create a supportive environment for self-acceptance
To reinforce desired behaviours through token rewards
questions.explain: Psychoanalytic therapy aims to bring unconscious conflicts, impulses, and repressed memories to awareness so their control over behaviour is reduced. This is fundamentally different from cognitive approaches (rational thought replacement), behavioural approaches (learning new responses), or person-centred approaches (self-acceptance in supportive environment).

questions.q: How do psychoanalytic and person-centered therapy differ in their time orientation?
options: Psychoanalytic focuses on the present; person-centered focuses on the past
Psychoanalytic is past-focused and prolonged; person-centered is present/future-focused
Both focus equally on past, present, and future
Psychoanalytic focuses on behaviour; person-centered focuses on cognition
Neither approach considers time important
questions.explain: Psychoanalytic therapy is deeply past-focused, exploring childhood conflicts and unconscious history — it is typically prolonged and expensive. Person-centered therapy emphasizes the present and future, creating a supportive environment for self-discovery now and growth going forward.

questions.q: What does 'unconditional positive regard' mean in person-centered therapy?
options: The therapist only values the client if they make progress
The therapist accepts and supports the client without judgment or conditions
The therapist praises only the client's rational thoughts
The therapist rewards the client with tokens or privileges
The therapist challenges all of the client's beliefs directly
questions.explain: Unconditional positive regard is the core technique of person-centered therapy — the therapist provides support, acceptance, and non-judgmental attention regardless of the client's behaviours, thoughts, or progress. This creates a safe environment for self-discovery and self-acceptance. It is fundamentally different from conditional reinforcement (tokens) or challenging beliefs.

questions.q: According to the lecture, what is the 'treatment gap' in mental health?
options: The difference in cost between psychotherapy and medication
The time delay between diagnosis and beginning treatment
The significant gap between people with mental health conditions and those receiving treatment
The difference in effectiveness between psychological and medical treatments
The gap in quality of care between different countries
questions.explain: The treatment gap refers to the fact that most people with a mental health condition receive no treatment at all. This is a major public health challenge, despite the evidence that psychotherapy is effective. The lecture emphasizes this gap as central to understanding barriers to care.

questions.q: Which 'common factors' are identified as responsible for improvement across different therapy orientations?
options: Medication combined with therapy
Empathy, hope, new ways of thinking/feeling/behaving, connecting with others
Exposure to feared stimuli
Challenging unconscious conflicts only
Token rewards and reinforcement
questions.explain: Across all therapy orientations (behavioural, cognitive, psychoanalytic, person-centred), common factors such as empathy, hope, new ways of thinking/feeling/behaving, and connecting with others drive improvement. These transcend the specific techniques or theoretical orientation. This is distinct from technique-specific factors.

questions.q: For which of the following disorders does CBT have a large effect size?
options: Autism spectrum disorder, bipolar disorder, and schizophrenia
Depression, generalized anxiety disorder, panic disorder, and PTSD
Only specific phobias, not other anxiety disorders
Personality disorders exclusively
Only childhood disorders, not adult disorders
questions.explain: According to Butler et al. (2006), CBT has large effect sizes for depression, generalized anxiety disorder (GAD), panic disorder, social phobia, PTSD, and childhood depressive and anxiety disorders. The exam trap is assuming CBT is equally effective for all disorders — it is not.

questions.q: What are 'system factors' as barriers to mental health treatment?
options: The client's personal beliefs and stigma about mental illness
Cost, policy/legal constraints, and too few mental health providers
The client's cultural background and family attitudes
The therapist's theoretical orientation and training
The length of time required for therapy to be effective
questions.explain: System factors are structural barriers including cost of services, policy and legal constraints, and insufficient providers. Attitudinal factors are distinct — they include mental health literacy, stigma, and cultural/ethnic influences. Together, system and attitudinal factors create the treatment gap.

questions.q: What is the relationship between mental health literacy and treatment-seeking behaviour?
options: Mental health literacy has no connection to whether people seek treatment
Poor mental health literacy is an attitudinal barrier that contributes to the treatment gap
Mental health literacy only affects medication-seeking, not therapy-seeking
Mental health literacy is purely a system factor, not attitudinal
High mental health literacy guarantees that people will have access to treatment
questions.explain: Mental health literacy — awareness and understanding of mental health conditions and treatments — is identified as an attitudinal factor. People with poor mental health literacy may not recognize problems or may not know where to seek help, contributing to the treatment gap. Unlike system factors (cost, providers), literacy is about attitudes and knowledge.

questions.q: According to Kazdin (2023), which of the following is NOT listed as a barrier to mental health treatment?
options: Cost of services
Stigma
Too few providers
Ineffectiveness of all therapy approaches
Policy and legal constraints
questions.explain: The lecture explicitly identifies system factors (cost, policy, providers) and attitudinal factors (literacy, stigma, culture) as barriers. The ineffectiveness of therapy is NOT a barrier mentioned — in fact, the lecture establishes that psychotherapy IS effective. This is an exam trap; the barrier is not that therapy doesn't work, but that access is limited.

questions.q: What does 'digital health' as a category encompass?
options: Only video conferencing and remote monitoring
Psychotherapy delivered exclusively online
Health IT, mHealth, telehealth, and advanced modalities (AR/VR)
Only mental health applications and wellness apps
Only therapeutic services, not administrative healthcare services
questions.explain: Digital health is a broad umbrella category including health IT (electronic records, secure messaging), mHealth (apps, wearables), telehealth (video, VOIP, remote monitoring), and advanced modalities (AR/VR, digital therapeutics). Computer-based psychotherapy is a sub-category within digital health, not synonymous with it.

questions.q: Which of the following is an example of a digital health application that is NOT computer-based psychotherapy?
options: Mobile Mood Diary app for tracking mood and sleep
VR exposure therapy for social anxiety
CBM game app for attention retraining
Electronic health records and secure messaging
An app that guides exposure exercises
questions.explain: Electronic health records and secure messaging are part of health IT, which is a component of digital health but not computer-based psychotherapy. The other options are all examples of psychotherapy delivered or supported digitally. This tests the understanding that digital health is broader than psychotherapy.

questions.q: What learning effect is described for VR exposure therapy for eating disorders?
options: Heights are safe and I can manage vertical spaces
I can manage a healthy approach to food
I am not as socially anxious as I thought
I no longer need to avoid certain foods
VR exposure has no learning effect on eating disorders
questions.explain: The lecture describes VR exposure to food leading to the learning effect 'I can manage a healthy approach to food' and changes in thoughts about food. For heights, the learning effect is 'Heights are safe.' For social anxiety, exposure in a virtual restaurant teaches about managing social interactions. Each VR application targets a specific learning outcome.

questions.q: How did the COVID-19 pandemic affect video tele-mental health visits in the Veterans Health Administration (VHA)?
options: Video visits decreased sharply while face-to-face visits surged
Face-to-face visits remained stable while video visits increased slightly
Face-to-face visits dropped sharply while video-to-home visits surged
Tele-mental health was discontinued entirely
No meaningful change in either type of visit occurred
questions.explain: During COVID-19, the VHA experienced a sharp decline in face-to-face mental health visits paired with a large surge in video-to-home visits. This reflects the pandemic-driven shift to telehealth. Before COVID, VHA video visits had already increased eightfold in the prior decade.

questions.q: Which therapy orientation emphasizes helping the client discover irrational thoughts through questioning rather than directly telling them their thoughts are wrong?
options: Psychoanalytic therapy with free association
Behavioural therapy with token economy
Cognitive therapy using the Socratic style
Person-centered therapy with unconditional positive regard
Aversion therapy with stimulus pairing
questions.explain: The Socratic/teacher-guided style of cognitive therapy involves the therapist asking guided questions to help clients discover disconfirming evidence and realize their thoughts are irrational (e.g., 'my husband doesn't love me' by testing the evidence). This differs from the confrontational style, which directly attacks beliefs. It also differs from other orientations' core methods.

questions.q: What is the primary therapeutic mechanism of systematic desensitization?
options: Extinction of conditioned fear response through habituation
Counterconditioning via pairing relaxation with increasing exposure
Cognitive restructuring of anxious thoughts
Release of unconscious conflicts through free association
Reinforcement of adaptive behaviour with rewards
questions.explain: Systematic desensitization works through counterconditioning — the client learns to associate the feared stimulus with relaxation rather than anxiety, enabling gradual tolerance of increasing exposure. This is distinct from exposure therapy, which relies on habituation and extinction without relaxation pairing.

questions.q: Which of the following best describes the relationship between psychotherapy and medication as treatments for psychological disorders?
options: Medication is always superior to psychotherapy
Psychotherapy is always superior to medication
Both are valid treatment approaches that operate through different mechanisms and may be combined
Medication treats disorders while psychotherapy treats only problems in living
Neither approach has demonstrated effectiveness
questions.explain: The lecture establishes that psychological disorders can be treated with either psychotropic medications (chemical mechanism) or psychotherapy (psychological mechanism). Both treat disorders and may be combined. Neither is categorically superior; effectiveness depends on the specific disorder and client factors.

questions.q: According to Norcross & Goldfried (2005), what percentage of therapists identified their approach as integrative or eclectic?
options: More than 95%
questions.explain: The lecture cites Norcross & Goldfried (2005) data showing that 13%–42% of therapists identify their approach as integrative or eclectic, combining multiple therapy orientations. This demonstrates that pure single-orientation approaches are not the only practice model used by therapists.

lectures.title: Lecture 7: What Makes a Good Parent?

questions.q: According to Baumrind (1991), parenting styles are defined by which two dimensions?
options: Warmth and strictness
Responsiveness and demandingness
Affection and discipline
Involvement and control
Praise and criticism
questions.explain: Responsiveness and demandingness are the two foundational dimensions that define parenting styles. Responsiveness refers to how warmly parents react to children's needs, while demandingness refers to the degree of control and discipline imposed. These create the 2×2 grid for the four main styles.

questions.q: Which parenting style combines high responsiveness and high demandingness?
options: Permissive
Authoritarian
Authoritative
Uninvolved
Indifferent
questions.explain: Authoritative parenting is characterized by high responsiveness (warmth) and high demandingness (control). This combination produces positive child outcomes: good social skills, self-reliance, and independence. Do not confuse with Authoritarian, which is low responsiveness + high demandingness.

questions.q: Parents who use reasoning, encourage independence, and set clear limits while being warm exemplify which parenting style?
options: Uninvolved parenting
Permissive parenting
Authoritarian parenting
Authoritative parenting
Dismissive parenting
questions.explain: This behavior profile—firmness with warmth, reasoning, and encouragement of independence—is the textbook definition of authoritative parenting. These parents combine discipline (demandingness) with emotional responsiveness, leading to children who are socially skilled and self-reliant.

questions.q: Authoritarian parents (專制式) typically produce children who are:
options: Self-reliant and independent
Socially skilled and likable
Unsociable, unfriendly, and withdrawn
Immature and dependent
Confident and assertive
questions.explain: Authoritarian parenting (low responsiveness, high demandingness) results in children who are unsociable, unfriendly, and withdrawn. This contrasts sharply with authoritative parenting outcomes, which include good social skills and likability. The lack of warmth in authoritarian style compromises social development.

questions.q: Which parenting style is characterized by lax, inconsistent, and undemanding parenting with high responsiveness?
options: Authoritative
Authoritarian
Uninvolved
Permissive
Strict
questions.explain: Permissive parenting combines high responsiveness (warmth) with low demandingness (few rules or limits). Permissive parents are warm but inconsistent and undemanding. Children in this style tend to be immature, moody, dependent, and show low self-control.

questions.q: A parent says: 'You'll need to clean your room before we can go to the restaurant. As soon as you finish, we'll leave.' Which parenting style does this exemplify?
options: Permissive
Uninvolved
Authoritarian
Authoritative
Indulgent
questions.explain: This example demonstrates authoritative parenting: the parent sets a clear rule (high demandingness) and explains the consequence (using reasoning), while the promise of the restaurant trip conveys warmth and responsiveness. The combination of firmness with explanation is characteristic of authoritative style.

questions.q: Psychological control in parenting includes all of the following EXCEPT:
options: Guilt induction
Love withdrawal
Media monitoring
Shaming
Invalidation of feelings
questions.explain: Media monitoring is a form of behavioral control, not psychological control. Psychological control involves manipulation of the child's thoughts, feelings, and emotions (guilt, love withdrawal, shaming, invalidation). Behavioral control is rule-setting and monitoring, which generally predicts better outcomes.

questions.q: Which form of parental control generally predicts worse developmental outcomes?
options: Behavioral control
Rule-setting
Activity monitoring
Psychological control
Disclosure solicitation
questions.explain: Psychological control (manipulating thoughts and feelings through guilt, shaming, love withdrawal) predicts worse outcomes. In contrast, behavioral control (rules, monitoring, requesting information) predicts better outcomes. Both are 'control,' but they have opposite effects on child development.

questions.q: A parent tells their child: 'If you don't get an A on this test, I won't love you anymore.' This is an example of which control dimension?
options: Behavioral control
Positive reinforcement
Psychological control
Cognitive control
Permissive control
questions.explain: Love withdrawal is a classic example of psychological control—the parent manipulates the child's emotions and sense of security to enforce compliance. This intrusive, emotion-focused control predicts poor developmental outcomes, unlike behavioral control which sets clear rules and consequences.

questions.q: Behavioral control differs from psychological control in that behavioral control:
options: Manipulates a child's emotional security
Involves guilt induction and shaming
Sets clear rules and monitors activities
Withdraws parental affection
Is always harmful to development
questions.explain: Behavioral control is rule-setting and monitoring (requesting disclosure, media monitoring, etc.), which generally predicts better outcomes. Psychological control manipulates emotions. Though both are forms of 'control,' they have opposite developmental effects, so understanding this distinction is critical.

questions.q: Cross-cultural research has revealed a paradox regarding Chinese parenting: Chinese parents are often described as authoritarian, yet:
options: Chinese children show poor academic performance
Chinese children exhibit high anxiety
Chinese students perform well academically
Chinese children have insecure attachment
Chinese children struggle with peer relationships
questions.explain: Chao (1994) and other cross-cultural researchers found that authoritarian parenting in Chinese families does not predict poor school achievement as it does for European-Americans. This challenges the Western assumption that authoritarian style is universally harmful, revealing the importance of cultural context.

questions.q: In which contexts is authoritarian parenting MOST likely to be adaptive rather than maladaptive?
options: Wealthy suburban neighborhoods
Urban areas with excellent schools
Asian societies and dangerous neighborhoods
High-income professional families
Communities with low crime rates
questions.explain: Authoritarian parenting may be adaptive in Asian societies (where it is culturally normative) and in dangerous or violent neighborhoods (where strict control enhances safety). In these contexts, the negative effects observed in Western samples are reduced or absent, highlighting context-dependency.

questions.q: According to Ainsworth et al. (1978), the Strange Situation procedure measures:
options: Parental stress levels
Infant cognitive development
Attachment security
Language development
Motor milestones
questions.explain: The Strange Situation is the classic paradigm for measuring attachment. It observes the infant's behavior during separation from and reunion with the mother, across episodes involving a stranger. These behaviors reveal the security of the attachment bond.

questions.q: In the Strange Situation, what is the PRIMARY purpose of introducing a stranger?
options: To assess the infant's language skills
To measure the infant's sociability with unfamiliar people
To provide a controlled context for observing attachment behavior and stress
To test the infant's ability to follow instructions
To evaluate the infant's cognitive abilities
questions.explain: The stranger's presence creates a mildly stressful situation that reveals how the infant copes and whether they use the mother as a secure base. This helps distinguish attachment patterns based on response to unfamiliarity and separation stress.

questions.q: Approximately what percentage of infants display secure attachment in the Strange Situation?
questions.explain: Approximately 60% of infants show secure attachment, 20% insecure-avoidant, and 20% insecure-anxious/resistant. These prevalence rates are well-established in the attachment literature and represent the distribution across most Western samples.

questions.q: Which attachment type involves the infant showing no distress when the mother leaves but actively avoiding contact upon reunion?
options: Secure attachment
Insecure-anxious/resistant
Insecure-disorganized
Insecure-avoidant
Ambivalent attachment
questions.explain: Insecure-avoidant infants (約20%) show minimal distress at separation and actively avoid contact when the mother returns. This is NOT a sign of healthy independence but rather avoidance and suppression of distress—a key exam trap. Their caregivers tend to be rejecting or withdrawn.

questions.q: Secure attachment in infancy predicts all of the following in later life EXCEPT:
options: Greater sociability and peer acceptance
More advanced emotional understanding
More persistent effort on challenging tasks
Higher likelihood of avoidant romantic relationships
Less aggression and psychopathology
questions.explain: Secure attachment predicts sociability, emotional understanding, persistence, and reduced aggression/psychopathology. Securely attached individuals tend to develop secure romantic relationships, NOT avoidant ones. Avoidant attachment in adulthood is associated with insecure childhood attachment patterns.

questions.q: According to attachment theory, early attachment experiences primarily shape:
options: Physical growth patterns
Cognitive intelligence levels
How children interpret and respond to social experiences in later life
Genetic expression
Language acquisition rate
questions.explain: Long-term outcomes of early attachment show that attachment experiences shape social and emotional functioning by influencing how children interpret and respond to social situations later in life. This foundation affects friendships, emotional regulation, and relationship patterns into adulthood.

questions.q: What is the primary antecedent (predecessor) of secure attachment according to Bowlby?
options: Frequent separation from the mother
Strict discipline and high demands
A history of sensitive and responsive interactions between caregiver and child
Early exposure to structured education
Regular interaction with multiple caregivers
questions.explain: Secure attachment is rooted in a consistent history of sensitive (敏感的) and responsive parenting. When caregivers reliably respond to the infant's needs, secure attachment develops. In contrast, rejecting or unreliably available caregivers produce insecure patterns.

questions.q: Mothers of insecure-avoidant children typically exhibit which parenting behavior?
options: Inconsistent availability
Excessive warmth and permissiveness
Rejection or withdrawal from contact
Over-involvement in play
Anxious hovering
questions.explain: Mothers of avoidant children tend to reject the infant or withdraw from contact. This pattern of rejection leads the child to suppress their attachment needs and avoid seeking comfort. In contrast, mothers of anxious-resistant children are inconsistently available, producing the opposite pattern of clinginess and resistance.

questions.q: The ABC (Attachment and Biobehavioral Catch-up) intervention targets which three caregiver behaviors?
options: Praise, encouragement, and discipline
Sensitivity to distress, following the child's lead, and reduced frightening behavior
Rule-setting, monitoring, and verbal instruction
Playfulness, teaching, and limit-setting
Affection, consistency, and independence-granting
questions.explain: ABC targets three specific behaviors: sensitivity to the child's distress, following the child's lead (rather than imposing the parent's agenda), and reducing frightening behaviors like yelling or grabbing. These interventions have cascading effects on inhibitory control, emotion regulation, and peer relations.

questions.q: VIPP-SD differs from ABC in its primary intervention method. What is VIPP-SD's key strategy?
options: Classroom-based instruction for parents
Video feedback to support sensitive parenting and firm limit-setting
Home visiting and medication
Play therapy with the child
Parent support groups and discussion
questions.explain: VIPP-SD (Video-feedback Intervention to Promote Positive Parenting and Sensitive Discipline) uses video feedback to help parents see their interactions and modify parenting behavior toward more sensitivity and appropriate discipline. This differs from ABC, which focuses on directly coaching three specific behaviors.

questions.q: Intergenerational transmission refers to:
options: Genetic inheritance of physical traits only
The transfer of abilities, traits, behaviors, and outcomes from parents to children
The legal transfer of property between generations
Conflict between parents and children
Cultural differences between age groups
questions.explain: Intergenerational transmission is the process by which parenting styles, attachment patterns, and behaviors pass from one generation to the next. It occurs through multiple mechanisms: genetics, socioeconomic environment, deliberate instruction, and observational learning.

questions.q: Which of the following is an example of child-to-parent intergenerational transmission?
options: A parent teaching a child how to solve math problems
A mother's depression affecting her parenting and the child's mental health
Children exposed to aggression learning to use coercion and accepting it as normal
A parent setting household rules
A parent encouraging independence in their child
questions.explain: When children exposed to inter-parental aggression learn to use coercion and aggression as conflict-resolution strategies, they are transmitting this learned behavior back to their parents and into their own future families. This exemplifies bidirectional transmission, not only parent-to-child.

questions.q: Social referencing is the process by which an infant:
options: Learns to walk by imitating parents
Refers to another person's expressions to determine how to appraise a situation
Develops a sense of self
Learns language from caregivers
Forms a secure attachment bond
questions.explain: Social referencing is specifically the process of looking to a caregiver's emotional expression to interpret an ambiguous or novel situation. The classic example is the visual cliff experiment (Sorce et al., 1985): infants crossed the cliff more often when the mother smiled and avoided it when she posed fear.

questions.q: In Klinnert's (1981) classic social referencing study, infants were more likely to approach novel toys when:
options: The toy had bright colors
The mother smiled
Other infants were playing with the toy
The room was familiar
The toy made noise
questions.explain: Klinnert found that infants' approach to novel toys depended on the mother's facial expression: they approached when she smiled, avoided when she showed fear, and showed mixed reactions to neutral expressions. This demonstrates that infants use social referencing to determine appropriate responses.

questions.q: The visual cliff experiment (Sorce et al., 1985) demonstrated that infants are more likely to cross a visual cliff when the mother expresses which emotions?
options: Sadness and disappointment
Joy and interest
Confusion and uncertainty
Surprise and caution
Anger and frustration
questions.explain: When the mother posed joy or interest, most infants crossed the deep side of the visual cliff. When she posed fear or anger, very few crossed. This study is a landmark demonstration of social referencing: infants rely on caregiver expressions to appraise risk and decide whether to explore.

questions.q: Parental math anxiety (父母數學焦慮) is associated with poorer child math outcomes, especially when:
options: The parent praises the child's effort
The parent provides minimal homework help
The anxious parent provides more homework help
The parent uses fixed mindset language
The child attends public school
questions.explain: Maloney et al. (2015) found that anxious parents who provided MORE homework help actually transmitted their anxiety and negative attitudes to children, worsening outcomes. The interaction during homework—where the parent expressed frustration—was the mechanism of transmission, not the homework help itself.

questions.q: Fixed mindset parents tend to give what type of praise, and what learning orientation does this foster?
options: Process praise; mastery orientation
Person praise; performance orientation
Effort praise; growth orientation
Ability praise; intrinsic motivation
Behavioral praise; cooperative learning
questions.explain: Fixed mindset parents (who believe ability is fixed) give more person praise ('you are smart'), which fosters performance orientation. Growth mindset parents give more process praise ('I like your effort'), which fosters mastery orientation and persistence. These praise styles shape children's mindset and learning goals.

questions.q: Growth mindset parents differ from fixed mindset parents in that growth mindset parents tend to:
options: Emphasize innate ability
Give more person-focused praise
Believe ability is changeable and give process-focused praise
Focus on grades and test scores
Encourage competitive achievement
questions.explain: Growth mindset parents ('ability is changeable') emphasize process praise ('effort,' 'strategies') which fosters mastery goals and persistence in children. Fixed mindset parents emphasize person traits ('smart,' 'talented'), fostering performance goals. Research by Gunderson et al. (2012, 2013) links these to children's own mindsets.

lectures.title: Lecture 8: Why Do Some People Handle Stress Better Than Others?

questions.q: According to Lazarus (1966), which element is essential to the definition of stress?
options: The occurrence of an objectively dangerous event
An individual's perception that they cannot adequately cope with demands
A consistent physiological response across all people
The presence of a traumatic stressor lasting more than one day
An automatic fight-or-flight reaction
questions.explain: Lazarus's definition emphasizes perception and appraisal — stress arises when individuals perceive they cannot cope, not based on the objective nature of the event. The most common wrong answer is the first option, as students often think stress requires an objectively dangerous situation.

questions.q: Which of the following best illustrates the perceptual nature of stress?
options: A person experiencing physical pain always reports high stress
The same public speaking event may be threatening to one person but challenging to another
Traumatic events produce identical stress responses in everyone
Stressors are exclusively external demands placed on a person
Biological stress responses do not vary between individuals
questions.explain: Stress is perceptual — the same event is appraised differently by different people. Option B demonstrates this key principle. Options A, C, and E are contradicted by evidence; option D misses the role of individual perception.

questions.q: What is the primary distinction between stressors and stress?
options: Stressors are always negative events, while stress can be positive
Stress is the objective threat, while stressors are the psychological perception
Stressors are sources of demand or threat, while stress is the state that arises from that perception
Stressors only occur during catastrophes, while stress occurs from all four types of events
Stressors are measurable, while stress is not
questions.explain: Stressors are the external sources (demands, threats); stress is the internal state that arises when an individual perceives inability to cope. Options A and B reverse or misdefine these concepts; option C correctly distinguishes cause from effect.

questions.q: Which category of stressors is characterized by unpredictability and large-scale effects, such as natural disasters or terrorist attacks?
options: Traumatic events
Major life events
Catastrophes
Hassles
Occupational stressors
questions.explain: Catastrophes are specifically unpredictable, large-scale events threatening many people at once. Traumatic events involve actual or threatened death but may be individual (assault, combat); major life events have fading consequences; hassles are minor; occupational stressors are work-related.

questions.q: According to the Social Readjustment Rating Scale (Holmes & Rahe, 1967), which life event typically carries the highest life change units?
options: Dismissal from work
Death of a close family member
Change in financial state
Beginning or ending school
Change in working hours or conditions
questions.explain: The table in the notes shows death of a close family member at 63 life change units, the highest among all listed events. This is recall-based on the provided data.

questions.q: Which statement correctly reflects the relationship between major life events and cumulative stress?
options: Only negative major life events contribute to life change units
Major life events like personal achievement also carry life change units and contribute to cumulative stress
Major life events are never measured on the SRRS scale
Only events over 50 life change units are considered stressors
Positive events always reduce overall stress burden
questions.explain: An exam trap: the SRRS includes positive events (personal achievement, school completion) that still carry life change units and add to cumulative stress. Stress is cumulative regardless of valence, not just from negative events.

questions.q: What is a key characteristic of occupational stress experienced by nurses, as described in the lecture?
options: Lack of advancement opportunities and unsupportive supervisors
Work overload, heavy physical demands, and dealing with death
Excessive paperwork and lack of parental support
Unpredictable and extreme job nature with inexperience
Little positive feedback and unsafe environments
questions.explain: The notes specifically list work overload, heavy physical demands, dealing with death, and interpersonal conflict as stressors for nurses. Other options correctly describe stressors for different occupational groups (social workers, emergency workers, teachers, clerical workers).

questions.q: According to Arnold & Fletcher (2012), professional athletes face organizational stressors in how many main categories?
options: Two: performance and team issues
Three: leadership, logistical, and performance issues
Four: leadership, logistical, performance, and cultural issues
Five: environmental, social, competitive, health, and financial issues
Six: including both personal and organizational dimensions
questions.explain: The lecture notes explicitly state four categories: (1) leadership and personnel issues, (2) logistical and environmental issues, (3) performance and personal issues, (4) cultural and team issues.

questions.q: What does the statistic from Galea et al. (2002) regarding PTSD after 9/11 primarily demonstrate?
options: PTSD affected 100% of people exposed to the terrorist attack
Proximity to the stressor significantly influenced PTSD prevalence (20% near Ground Zero vs. 7.5% further north)
PTSD only develops in individuals with prior trauma
Distance from a catastrophe has no effect on PTSD rates
Exactly half of all disaster survivors develop PTSD
questions.explain: The data clearly shows a dose-response relationship: greater proximity to Ground Zero (20%) produced higher PTSD rates than distance (7.5%), demonstrating the importance of direct exposure to catastrophic stressors.

questions.q: According to Lazarus & Folkman (1984), what is the primary purpose of primary appraisal in the stress process?
options: To evaluate one's ability to cope with the event
To determine whether an event is threatening or challenging
To activate the fight-or-flight response immediately
To seek social support from others
To suppress emotional reactions
questions.explain: Primary appraisal specifically determines whether an event is perceived as threatening or as a challenge (opportunity for gain/growth). Secondary appraisal evaluates coping ability. The exam trap is confusing these two distinct cognitive steps.

questions.q: In the two-stage appraisal model, which outcome occurs when secondary appraisal reveals no effective coping options available?
options: Low threat perception and adaptive coping
Challenge perception and increased motivation
High threat perception and stress response
Automatic problem-solving and resolution
Emotional suppression and avoidance
questions.explain: When secondary appraisal reveals ineffective or no options to cope, threat perception increases. This is distinct from challenge perception, which occurs when coping options seem viable. Options A and B misrepresent the outcome of ineffective coping options.

questions.q: How does the distinction between challenge and threat appraisal relate to psychological outcomes?
options: They are essentially the same perception with different names
Challenge appraisal involves potential for gain, while threat involves potential for harm or loss
Threat is always more adaptive than challenge
Only threat appraisal activates coping mechanisms
Challenge appraisal never occurs in genuinely stressful situations
questions.explain: Challenge appraisal (perceived potential for growth) and threat appraisal (perceived potential for harm) represent distinct primary appraisals with different emotional and behavioral outcomes. This distinction drives different secondary appraisals.

questions.q: Which physiological response is characteristic of adaptive short-term stress as described in the lecture?
options: Decreased heart rate and blood pressure
Suppression of hormone secretion by the adrenal glands
Increased heart rate, blood pressure, and activation via fight-or-flight response
Immune system shutdown and tissue degradation
Permanent elevation of cortisol levels
questions.explain: Adaptive short-term stress mobilizes the body through increased heart rate, blood pressure, hormone secretion, and skin conductance changes. Prolonged exposure causes the harmful effects mentioned in other options.

questions.q: What is the critical difference between short-term and prolonged exposure to stress?
options: Short-term stress causes exhaustion while prolonged stress does not
Short-term stress mobilizes adaptive responses while prolonged exposure leads to deterioration and illness
They produce identical physiological outcomes
Short-term stress never activates the fight-or-flight response
Prolonged stress only affects mental health, not physical health
questions.explain: Short-term stress is adaptive and mobilizing; prolonged exposure causes decline in bodily functioning, tissue deterioration, and decreased immune functioning. This is the key mechanism explaining why stress becomes harmful over time.

questions.q: According to Selye's (1956) General Adaptation Syndrome, what characterizes the resistance stage?
options: The body's initial detection and response to a stressor
The body meets and actively resists the stressor
The body's coping reserves become depleted
Complete recovery and return to baseline functioning
Activation of the parasympathetic nervous system
questions.explain: In the resistance stage, the body is actively coping with and resisting the stressor. The alarm stage involves initial detection; exhaustion involves depletion of coping reserves. Each stage is functionally distinct.

questions.q: What does the exhaustion stage of General Adaptation Syndrome NOT represent?
options: Depletion of the body's coping reserves
A state where negative health consequences emerge from inadequate stress resistance
Ordinary fatigue from physical exercise or normal exertion
Increased susceptibility to illness due to prolonged stress
Consequences of inadequate coping when stressor persists
questions.explain: An exam trap: the exhaustion stage specifically means depletion of coping resources and emergence of illness, not ordinary fatigue. It is a pathological state resulting from prolonged, inadequately managed stress, not normal tiredness.

questions.q: In the Cohen et al. (1991) study on stress and colds, what was the key finding?
options: High-stress individuals never developed colds regardless of exposure
High-stress individuals were more likely to develop colds even after controlling for personality and health
Stress had no measurable effect on infection risk
Only personality traits, not stress, predicted cold susceptibility
All participants developed colds at the same rate
questions.explain: The study demonstrated a direct link between high stress and increased cold development, even when other factors were controlled. This evidence supports the stress-immunity relationship central to psychoneuroimmunology.

questions.q: How does social support influence immune function during stressful periods like exam time?
options: Social support decreases antibody production
Strong social support is associated with higher antibody levels
Social support only affects emotional responses, not immune markers
Antibody levels are unaffected by stress or support
Only professional medical treatment improves antibody levels during stress
questions.explain: The Jemmott & Magloire (1988) study found that students with stronger social support during exams had higher antibody levels, demonstrating the protective effect of support on immune function during stress.

questions.q: What is the primary focus of psychoneuroimmunology as described in the lecture?
options: The study of brain anatomy and neurotransmitter chemistry
The study of relationships among psychological factors, the immune system, and the brain
The analysis of how the nervous system controls muscular contractions
The examination of genetic factors in disease resistance
The investigation of pharmaceutical treatments for immune disorders
questions.explain: Psychoneuroimmunology specifically examines how psychological factors interact with the immune system and brain. The lecture describes three pathways through which stress affects health, central to this field.

questions.q: According to the lecture, which pathway does NOT represent how stress affects health through psychoneuroimmunology?
options: Direct physiological effects like elevated blood pressure
Harmful behavioral changes like increased substance use
Genetic mutations directly caused by stress exposure
Decreased compliance with medical advice
Delayed or avoided help-seeking behavior
questions.explain: The lecture identifies three pathways: direct physiological effects, harmful behaviors, and indirect health-related behaviors. Genetic mutations caused by stress are not part of the psychoneuroimmunology model as presented.

questions.q: Which coping strategy involves taking action to reduce the stressor or prevent its recurrence?
options: Avoidance-oriented coping
Problem-focused coping
Emotion-focused coping
Wishful thinking
Direct escape
questions.explain: Problem-focused coping targets the stressor directly through action (consulting professionals, acquiring information). Avoidance-oriented coping postpones dealing with the problem; emotion-focused coping manages emotions rather than addressing the source.

questions.q: Under what circumstances is emotion-focused coping considered the most adaptive choice?
options: Whenever any stressor is present
In controllable, modifiable situations
In genuinely unchangeable or uncertain circumstances
Only as a last resort after problem-focused strategies fail
It is never as adaptive as other strategies
questions.explain: The lecture explicitly states emotion-focused coping is best used for unchangeable or uncertain circumstances. An exam trap: emotion-focused coping is not inherently inferior — it is the appropriate match to uncontrollable situations, where problem-focused coping may increase anxiety.

questions.q: What does coping flexibility (Cheng, 2001) emphasize as the key to effective stress management?
options: Using the same coping strategy in all situations
Avoiding all emotional responses to stressors
Matching coping strategies to situational demands and controllability
Choosing problem-focused coping for all manageable situations
Eliminating the need for emotion-focused coping
questions.explain: Coping flexibility involves deploying different strategies appropriately across contexts. Rigidly applying problem-focused coping to uncontrollable situations creates anxiety; applying emotion-focused coping to controllable situations delays problem resolution. The key is matching strategy to situational demands.

questions.q: Why might problem-focused coping in an uncontrollable situation be counterproductive?
options: It always succeeds in solving the problem
It can elicit anxiety and waste resources on unsolvable problems
It suppresses emotional responses completely
It is the most adaptive approach in all contexts
It leads to automatic problem resolution
questions.explain: When a situation is genuinely uncontrollable, problem-focused coping efforts may increase frustration and anxiety because the stressor cannot be solved through action. Emotion regulation becomes the adaptive response.

questions.q: Which technique involves individuals learning to voluntarily alter their own bodily signals after viewing them?
options: Meditation and breathing exercises
Guided imagery
Biofeedback
Relaxation exercises
Contact with nature
questions.explain: Biofeedback specifically involves showing individuals their own bodily signals (heart rate, blood pressure) and teaching them strategies to voluntarily alter those signals. Other options are distinct stress reduction techniques.

questions.q: According to Ulrich's (1991) stress reduction theory, how does nature influence physiological responses?
options: Nature increases sympathetic nervous system activity and arousal
Nature automatically suppresses sympathetic nervous system activity and elicits positive reactions
Nature has no measurable effect on stress responses
Nature only affects mental health, not physiological stress
Nature requires active cognitive effort to reduce stress
questions.explain: Stress reduction theory proposes that nature automatically triggers positive reactions linked to suppression of sympathetic nervous system activity, an evolutionary adaptive response. This is distinct from deliberate relaxation techniques.

questions.q: What are the three types of social support identified in the lecture?
options: Physical, emotional, and intellectual support
Informational, materialistic, and emotional support
Professional, peer, and family support
Active, passive, and preventive support
Direct, indirect, and symbolic support
questions.explain: The lecture explicitly lists three types: informational support (advice/information), materialistic support (goods/services), and emotional support (feeling valued). The other options incorrectly categorize support types.

questions.q: How do pets exemplify the protective role of social support against stress, according to the lecture?
options: Pets have no measurable effect on stress responses
Women exposed to stress showed less physiological reaction when with their pets, demonstrating pets as a social support source
Pets only provide material support, not emotional support
Pets increase stress by adding responsibility
Pet ownership always requires professional guidance to be beneficial
questions.explain: The Allen et al. (1991) study showed that women with pets present exhibited less physiological reaction to stress, demonstrating that pets can serve as a source of social support. This illustrates the buffering effect of supportive relationships.

questions.q: What is the defining characteristic of psychological resilience as described by Block & Kremen (1996)?
options: The ability to avoid all stressors
A trait that can only be developed through professional therapy
The ability to overcome, steer through, and bounce back from adversity
An innate characteristic present from birth
The capacity to eliminate emotional responses to challenges
questions.explain: Psychological resilience is defined as a relatively stable trait involving the ability to overcome and recover from adversity. An exam trap: while described as stable, it emerges from modifiable psychological factors, so it is not purely innate.

questions.q: According to Fletcher & Sarkar (2012), which factor does NOT contribute to psychological resilience in Olympic champions?
options: Positive personality traits and optimism
Confidence in ability to succeed under pressure
Perceived social support
Absence of any stressors or challenges
Meta-cognitions and thinking about one's own strategies
questions.explain: The lecture lists positive personality, confidence, perceived social support, and meta-cognitions as resilience factors. Olympic champions face significant stressors — resilience is not the absence of challenges but the ability to overcome them despite stressors being present.

lectures.title: Lecture 9: Why Do We Need Friends?

questions.q: According to Baumeister and Leary's Need-to-Belong Theory, what do humans fundamentally seek in relationships?
options: Infrequent deep interactions with many acquaintances
Frequent affectively positive interactions within long-term caring relationships
Competitive opportunities to demonstrate superiority
Material resources and financial security
Intellectual debate and ideological agreement
questions.explain: Baumeister & Leary (1995) explicitly state that people seek frequent, affectively positive interactions within long-term, caring relationships. Infrequent or shallow interactions, competition, materialism, and debate are distractors that miss this core definition.

questions.q: In Self-Determination Theory, which of the following is NOT one of the three inherent psychological needs?
options: Autonomy
Competence
Security
Relatedness
Achievement
questions.explain: SDT identifies three needs: competence, relatedness, and autonomy.
