Security and achievement are not formal needs in this framework, though security may relate to basic safety (outside SDT) and achievement relates to competence. Students often forget autonomy and confuse SDT with other need theories.

questions.q: What does the exam trap in Self-Determination Theory emphasize?
options: Only two needs are required for well-being
Autonomy is optional for optimal well-being
All three needs—competence, relatedness, and autonomy—must be satisfied for optimal well-being
Relatedness is more important than competence
Autonomy can be substituted with external rewards
questions.explain: The exam trap warns that SDT requires all three needs simultaneously for optimal well-being. Students often forget autonomy or think two needs suffice. Partial satisfaction does not produce optimal well-being.

questions.q: In Maslow's Hierarchy of Needs, what is the correct ordering of the lowest three levels?
options: Belongingness → Safety → Physiological
Physiological → Belongingness → Safety
Physiological → Safety → Belongingness
Safety → Physiological → Belongingness
Belongingness → Physiological → Safety
questions.explain: Maslow's pyramid places Physiological (bottom) → Safety → Belongingness (level 3). The exam trap explicitly warns that belongingness is level 3, not level 2. Safety must be satisfied before social needs can be pursued.

questions.q: According to Maslow's hierarchy, what happens when lower-level needs are not met?
options: People immediately jump to higher needs
People experience regression to more basic levels and cannot focus on growth
Physiological needs automatically resynchronize with safety needs
Higher needs become easier to achieve
The hierarchy reverses itself
questions.explain: Maslow's theory states that unmet lower needs cause regression—people focus downward rather than progressing upward. Meeting lower needs enables progression to higher levels.

questions.q: Which evidence supports Maslow's hierarchy across 123 nations?
options: Tay & Diener (2011) found safety needs came before physiological needs
Tay & Diener (2011) found basic and safety needs were most likely fulfilled first, then social needs
Tay & Diener (2011) found belongingness was the foundational need
Tay & Diener (2011) found all levels were satisfied equally regardless of order
Tay & Diener (2011) found self-actualization was the primary driver
questions.explain: Tay & Diener (2011) studied 123 nations and confirmed Maslow's ordering: basic and safety needs fulfilled first among those with limited overall fulfillment, then social needs followed. This supports the hierarchical structure.

questions.q: From an evolutionary perspective, which of the following is NOT mentioned as a recurrent adaptive challenge that social bonding helped solve?
options: Predation avoidance
Resource acquisition
Offspring care
Artistic expression
Coalitionary conflict
questions.explain: The lecture lists four adaptive challenges: predation avoidance, resource acquisition, offspring care, and coalitionary conflict. Artistic expression is not mentioned as an evolutionary pressure for social bonding in this context.

questions.q: What does Terror Management Theory propose about the relationship between mortality awareness and social bonding?
options: Death awareness has no effect on relationship-seeking behavior
Reminders of death decrease attempts to form close relationships
Reminders of death increase attempts to initiate new close relationships and maintain existing ones
Only elderly people experience increased bonding from death reminders
Death awareness only affects individual survival strategies, not social behavior
questions.explain: Terror Management Theory specifically states that reminders of death increase attempts to initiate new close relationships and maintain existing ones. The exam trap warns not to confuse this with ostracism research or fear of rejection.

questions.q: Which post-9/11 finding is consistent with Terror Management Theory?
options: 10% of Americans reported stronger relationships
40% reported decreased attempts to help others
60% of Americans reported their relationships were stronger after the attack
All Americans immediately stopped forming new bonds
Social connection decreased significantly after the trauma
questions.explain: The lecture cites Morgan et al. (2011) and others reporting that 60% of Americans reported stronger relationships post-9/11, consistent with TMT's prediction that mortality reminders increase bonding and relationship maintenance.

questions.q: What behavioral change did 40% of Americans show post-9/11 according to the Terror Management Theory evidence?
options: Increased isolation and withdrawal
Increased attempts to do nice things for others
Decreased charitable giving
Reduced community participation
Increased aggression toward strangers
questions.explain: The evidence shows 40% of Americans increased attempts to do nice things for others post-9/11, reflecting heightened prosocial behavior driven by mortality salience—a key prediction of Terror Management Theory.

questions.q: In Holt-Lunstad et al. (2017), having high-quality close relationships is associated with decreased risk for which outcomes?
options: Decreased all-cause mortality and disease morbidities only
Increased sports injuries and accidents only
Decreased all-cause mortality and disease morbidities across multiple conditions
Mental illness exclusively
Only short-term physical illness
questions.explain: The core finding is that high-quality close relationships decrease risk for all-cause mortality and disease morbidities across multiple conditions. This broad protective effect is one of the lecture's main health claims.

questions.q: Which of the following is NOT one of the three dimensions of social connection identified by Holt-Lunstad et al. (2021)?
options: Structure (network size, roles, marital status)
Function (perceived or received support)
Quality (relationship satisfaction, strain)
Intensity (frequency of contact per week)
Frequency (how often interactions occur)
questions.explain: Holt-Lunstad et al. (2021) identify three dimensions: Structure, Function, and Quality. Intensity and frequency are not formally listed as separate dimensions; Structure encompasses network size and contact patterns instead.

questions.q: According to the lecture, the protective effect of social connection on mortality is comparable to or exceeds which known health interventions?
options: Only smoking cessation in cardiac patients
Smoking cessation, physical activity, and abstaining from excessive alcohol
All named health interventions combined equally
No health interventions—social connection is unique
Only obesity management
questions.explain: Holt-Lunstad et al. (2017) report that social connection's protective effect exceeds abstaining from alcohol, flu vaccination, and obesity management, and is comparable to smoking cessation and physical activity. The lecture lists these comparisons explicitly.

questions.q: Which of the following is an example of a psychological pathway through which social connection influences health outcomes?
options: Cardiovascular changes
Increased sleep quality
Reduced perceived stress and improved resilience
Enhanced immune function
Improved medication adherence
questions.explain: The lecture lists psychological factors as: perceived stress, depression, resilience, meaning/purpose, hopefulness, and sense of safety. Reduced stress and resilience are psychological pathways. Cardiovascular changes, sleep, and immune function are biological or behavioral pathways.

questions.q: According to the lecture, which three types of pathways link social connection to morbidity and mortality?
options: Cognitive, emotional, and social
Genetic, environmental, and behavioral
Psychological, behavioral, and biological
Molecular, cellular, and systemic
Internal, external, and situational
questions.explain: The exam trap and lecture explicitly state that social connection operates via three pathway types: psychological (stress, depression, meaning), behavioral (sleep, activity, nutrition), and biological (cardiovascular, neuroendocrine, immune). The exam trap warns against naming only one.

questions.q: In the Cyberball study by Williams et al. (2000), what was the primary task participants performed?
options: Solving mathematical puzzles competitively
Playing an online disc-throwing game with two bogus players
Negotiating resource distribution with other players
Answering trivia questions under time pressure
Collaborating to build a virtual structure
questions.explain: Williams et al. (2000) designed Cyberball as an online disc-throwing game where participants played with two bogus (computer-controlled) players. Ostracism was operationalized by withholding the disc from the real participant.

questions.q: Which brain finding from the Cyberball study challenges the notion that social pain is merely metaphorical?
options: Decreased activity in pain-processing areas
Heightened activity in brain cortex area associated with physical pain
No activation in any sensory regions
Activation only in reward centers
Activation in language processing areas only
questions.explain: The exam trap explicitly states that heightened activity in pain-processing brain regions (same as physical pain) shows real neural overlap—not mere metaphor. This is a key finding demonstrating that social exclusion activates actual pain circuits.

questions.q: What was a behavioral consequence of ostracism in the Cyberball study?
options: Increased assertiveness and independent decision-making
Greater conformity to others' wrong judgments
Improved mood and enhanced social confidence
Reduced susceptibility to peer influence
Heightened critical thinking and disagreement
questions.explain: Ostracized participants showed greater conformity to others' wrong judgments, suggesting that exclusion undermines independent judgment. This is adaptive for reaffiliation—conforming helps people regain acceptance.

questions.q: In Twenge et al. (2001), how did rejection affect participant aggression?
options: Rejected participants became less aggressive to avoid further isolation
Rejected participants gave higher noise intensity and longer duration to punish game losers
Rejection had no effect on subsequent aggressive behavior
Accepted participants became more aggressive than rejected ones
Aggression decreased proportionally with rejection severity
questions.explain: Twenge et al. (2001) found that after rejection feedback, participants later gave higher noise intensity and longer noise duration when punishing game losers. This shows rejection increases subsequent aggressive behavior.

questions.q: According to Leary et al. (2003), what was a common pattern in perpetrators of school shootings (1995–2001)?
options: All shooters had experienced recent academic failures only
At least 12 of 15 perpetrators had experienced chronic bullying, teasing, or rejection
Most perpetrators had no prior social difficulties
Rejection played no role in any shooting incidents
Only foreign-born students committed these acts
questions.explain: Leary et al. (2003) found that in at least 12 of 15 school shooting incidents, perpetrators had experienced a pattern of malicious teasing, bullying, or rejection. Additionally, ~50% had experienced a recent romantic breakup or other rejecting event.

questions.q: In Bernstein et al. (2008), what ability was enhanced in excluded participants?
options: Ability to detect false statements in written text
Ability to distinguish genuine happy expressions from fake smiles
Ability to solve complex mathematical problems
Ability to remember unrelated information
Ability to ignore facial expressions entirely
questions.explain: Bernstein et al. (2008) found that excluded participants showed enhanced sensitivity to distinguish genuine happy expressions from fake smiles when viewing faces. This heightened social signal detection facilitates reaffiliation attempts.

questions.q: Why do excluded individuals show enhanced smile authenticity detection according to the lecture?
options: They become more cynical and distrustful of others
It is a reaffiliation-seeking mechanism—they monitor social signals to regain acceptance
They are naturally better at reading faces
It reflects a permanent personality change from trauma
It has no adaptive purpose and is merely a side effect
questions.explain: The lecture interprets enhanced smile detection as a reaffiliation-seeking mechanism. Excluded people heighten their social signal detection to identify genuine acceptance and facilitate their return to the group.

questions.q: What does anthropomorphism mean in the context of social exclusion according to Epley et al. (2007, 2008)?
options: Blaming others for one's loneliness
Perceiving nonhumans as humanlike to compensate for lack of social connection
Using human language to describe nature
Applying human evolutionary principles to animals
Creating fictional characters for entertainment
questions.explain: Anthropomorphism as studied by Epley et al. is a compensatory mechanism: lacking social connection, people attribute humanlike mental states (intentions, emotions) to gadgets, pets, and supernatural agents to satisfy their belonging need.

questions.q: In Epley et al.'s anthropomorphism research, what did lonely people report compared to non-lonely people?
options: Less mental states perceived in inanimate objects
More mental states (intentions, emotions) perceived in gadgets
No difference in object perception
Greater interest in physical activity
Stronger preference for solitary hobbies
questions.explain: Lonely people perceive more mental states and human traits in gadgets than non-lonely people. This projection of humanness onto objects is interpreted as compensating for lack of human connection.

questions.q: According to Chen et al. (2008), what did excluded participants show when evaluating an anthropomorphized brand?
options: More negative attitudes toward branded products
More positive attitudes toward M&M's candy when the brand was anthropomorphized
Indifference to brand personality
Preference for non-anthropomorphized brands
Complete avoidance of candy products
questions.explain: Chen et al. (2008) found that excluded participants reported more positive attitudes toward M&M's when the brand was presented with humanlike characteristics. This demonstrates compensation for lost belonging through brand anthropomorphism.

questions.q: Which statement best distinguishes Terror Management Theory from ostracism and rejection research?
options: They are the same theory with different names
TMT is about death anxiety driving bonding; ostracism research is about consequences of social exclusion
Ostracism research predicts increased relationships; TMT predicts isolation
Both predict aggressive behavior as the primary response
Neither theory addresses social connection
questions.explain: The exam trap explicitly warns students not to confuse TMT (which links mortality awareness to increased bonding) with ostracism research (which studies consequences of exclusion). TMT is predictive (death → bonding); ostracism studies reactive outcomes to exclusion.

questions.q: When comparing the health impact of social connection across multiple pathways, what makes social connection's protective effect unusual?
options: It only affects mental health, not physical health
It operates through only one isolated biological mechanism
It involves simultaneous psychological, behavioral, and biological processes
It has a weaker effect than any single health intervention
It only benefits elderly populations
questions.explain: Social connection's uniqueness is that it operates through multiple simultaneous pathways—psychological, behavioral, and biological. The exam trap warns against naming only one. This multi-pathway effect may explain why it rivals or exceeds single-intervention outcomes.

questions.q: Which combination of evidence best supports the Need-to-Belong Theory's claim that lack of belonging causes severe deprivation?
options: Maslow's hierarchy shows belongingness is level 3
Cyberball study shows pain-like neural activation and behavioral changes; rejection studies show aggression; anthropomorphism shows compensatory mechanisms
Only evolutionary theory supports this claim
Maslow and SDT alone provide sufficient evidence
No evidence directly supports severe deprivation claims
questions.explain: Multiple findings support the severe deprivation claim: Cyberball's pain activation and conformity, rejection-aggression studies, violence correlates, and anthropomorphic compensation all demonstrate substantial consequences of excluded belonging—supporting Baumeister & Leary's original theory.

questions.q: Which of the following is most consistent with Self-Determination Theory's emphasis on autonomy as a necessary need?
options: People perform best when given external rewards only
Autonomy is nice but not essential for well-being
Employees with autonomy and competence but low relatedness show optimal engagement
All three needs—autonomy, competence, and relatedness—must be satisfied for optimal well-being
Autonomy is less important than the other two needs
questions.explain: SDT's core claim is that ALL three needs (autonomy, competence, relatedness) must be satisfied simultaneously for optimal well-being. Partial satisfaction (even two of three) does not produce optimal outcomes. The exam trap specifically warns students not to treat autonomy as optional.

questions.q: According to Williams & Nida (2011), what are the general consequences of social exclusion or ostracism?
options: Only positive emotional responses to motivate reengagement
Negative physiological, affective, cognitive, and behavioral consequences; excluded people attempt to reaffiliate
Permanent social withdrawal with no motivation to reconnect
Exclusively cognitive deficits with no affective impact
No measurable consequences beyond temporary mood changes
questions.explain: Williams & Nida (2011) establish that social exclusion unleashes negative physiological, affective, cognitive, and behavioral consequences across multiple domains. Importantly, excluded individuals do not simply withdraw; instead, they typically attempt to reaffiliate, which is demonstrated in subsequent studies (Cyberball conformity, smile sensitivity, anthropomorphism).

lectures.title: Lecture 10: Would You Trust Your Eyes or Follow the Crowd?

questions.q: Which of the following best defines social influence?
options: The use of physical force to change someone's behaviour
An individual's behaviour being shaped by the actions of other people or groups
The conscious decision to adopt another person's personality traits
A deliberate agreement between two people to change their attitudes
The involuntary biological response to environmental stimuli
questions.explain: Social influence is formally defined as the observation that an individual's behaviour is shaped by the actions of other people or groups, and it can occur both consciously and unconsciously. Option A confuses influence with coercion; C and D describe deliberate choice rather than the broader concept of influence. E describes a biological response unrelated to social contexts.

questions.q: In Chartrand & Bargh's (1999) automatic mimicry study, what was the key finding about participants' awareness of their own behaviour?
options: Participants were highly aware of copying confederates' gestures
Participants consciously decided which gestures to mimic
Participants copied gestures without awareness or intent
Participants refused to mimic behaviours they found uncomfortable
Participants only mimicked gestures they had seen before
questions.explain: The study demonstrated that mimicry occurs without awareness or intent — this is the defining feature of automatic (as opposed to deliberate) mimicry. The exam trap is that students often confuse unconscious mimicry with conscious imitation. Options A and B describe deliberate behaviour; C and D describe conscious refusal.

questions.q: What effect did automatic mimicry have on post-interaction ratings in the Chartrand & Bargh study?
options: Mimicked participants rated the interaction as less smooth
Mimicked participants reported lower liking of the confederate
Mimicked participants reported higher liking and smoother interactions
Mimicked participants requested the confederate to stop copying them
Mimicked participants showed increased anxiety during the interaction
questions.explain: Post-interaction ratings showed that mimicked participants reported higher liking and smoother interaction quality. This demonstrates a positive social outcome of unconscious mimicry — facilitation of communication and relationship building. Options A, B, D, and E describe negative or non-existent effects.

questions.q: According to the Van Baaren et al. (2004) study, what was the pro-social spillover effect of being mimicked?
options: Mimicked participants were more likely to criticize the confederate
Mimicked participants avoided helping others in subsequent tasks
Mimicked participants were significantly more likely to help pick up dropped pens
Mimicked participants requested compensation for the study
Mimicked participants showed decreased empathy toward others
questions.explain: Van Baaren et al. found that participants who had been mimicked were significantly more likely to help pick up accidentally dropped pens within 10 seconds. This demonstrates that unconscious mimicry produces pro-social spillover effects beyond the immediate interaction.

questions.q: What was the error rate when Asch's participants faced unanimous confederate opposition on an easy line-judgment task?
questions.explain: Asch's original findings showed a conformity error rate of 36.8% — participants conformed to the wrong answer more than a third of the time on an easy task where 99% of individuals answering alone were correct. This striking discrepancy is the core finding of the study.

questions.q: In Asch's conformity studies, how did increasing the number of confederates affect the conformity rate?
options: Conformity increased steadily as each new confederate was added
Conformity increased sharply then plateaued after approximately 3-4 opponents
Conformity decreased as more confederates were added
Group size had no effect on conformity rates
Conformity followed a random pattern unrelated to group size
questions.explain: Group size effects were not linear. Conformity increased as opponents increased but plateaued after approximately 3-4 opponents — adding more confederates beyond this point produced diminishing returns. This suggests an optimal pressure point rather than unlimited influence from group size.

questions.q: What happened to conformity rates in Asch's experiments when even one confederate broke ranks and gave the correct answer?
options: Conformity rates increased dramatically
Conformity rates remained unchanged
Conformity rates decreased sharply
The confederate was excluded from the study
Participants began to question the entire study design
questions.explain: The presence of a single dissenter (someone giving the correct answer) sharply reduced conformity. This finding is crucial because it shows that unanimity of the group is critical for maintaining conformity pressure — one break in consensus substantially weakens the effect.

questions.q: In the modern Swiss replication by Franzen & Mader (2023), what was the effect of providing monetary incentives for correct answers on conformity rates?
options: Incentives had no effect; conformity remained at 33%
Incentives increased conformity to 42%
Incentives reduced conformity from 33% to 25%
Incentives eliminated conformity entirely
Incentives caused participants to give random answers
questions.explain: The Swiss replication showed that while conformity persisted (33% error rate), it was responsive to incentives — offering money for correct answers reduced the rate to 25%. This indicates that conformity is not purely automatic but can be modulated by motivation.

questions.q: Which of the following best describes informational influence?
options: Conformity driven by concern about what others think of us
Conformity from wanting to form an accurate interpretation and behave correctly
Conformity driven by fear of punishment from authority figures
Conformity resulting from previous commitments or consistency needs
Conformity driven by admiration for a specific individual
questions.explain: Informational influence is conformity motivated by a desire for accuracy — people assume that if others agree, the group judgment must be correct, especially in ambiguous situations. This differs from normative influence, which is about social approval and belonging.

questions.q: When is informational influence most dominant according to the lecture material?
options: When social stakes are clear and public
When the individual values group membership highly
When the situation is ambiguous or difficult
When authority figures are present
When the task has been practiced extensively
questions.explain: Informational influence dominates in ambiguous or difficult situations where the person is uncertain and looks to others for cues about the correct interpretation. In contrast, normative influence dominates when there are clear social stakes and public visibility of the response.

questions.q: How do collectivistic and individualistic societies differ in their conformity rates according to Bond & Smith (1996)?
options: They show no differences in conformity
Individualistic societies conform more than collectivistic ones
Collectivistic societies show more conformity than individualistic ones
The relationship is random and unpredictable
Conformity rates are determined solely by age and education
questions.explain: Cross-cultural research shows that collectivistic societies (with emphasis on group harmony and belonging) exhibit higher conformity rates than individualistic societies. This reflects different cultural values regarding group interdependence.

questions.q: Which of the following is the best definition of compliance in the context of social influence?
options: Automatic mimicry of another person's gestures
Changing one's behaviour to match others in a group setting
Acquiescence or positive response to a direct or covert request
Unconscious adoption of group norms over time
Following written rules established by an organization
questions.explain: Compliance is specifically the response to a direct or covert (indirect) request, such as a sales pitch or donation request. It differs from conformity (which is about matching group responses) and from obedience (which involves commands from authority).

questions.q: According to Cialdini's six principles, which of the following is the mechanism of the reciprocation principle?
options: If many people are doing it, it must be right
We are attracted to people we like and similar to us
Rare or time-limited items seem more valuable
Normative pressure to repay what another has given
Desire to appear consistent with our past behaviour
questions.explain: Reciprocation is based on the normative pressure to repay what others have given us — exemplified by free gifts with purchase. Social Proof is 'everyone does it' (option A); Liking is about attraction (B); Scarcity is about rarity (C); Commitment/Consistency is about past behaviour (E).

questions.q: Which of Cialdini's six principles operates through informational influence rather than normative influence?
options: Reciprocation
Liking
Authority
Social Proof
Scarcity
questions.explain: Social Proof operates via informational influence — if everyone is doing it, it must be right. This is an accuracy-based judgment. The exam trap is that students often assign Social Proof to normative influence because it involves 'others,' but the mechanism is informational (about what's correct), not approval-seeking.

questions.q: What is the foot-in-the-door technique and which of Cialdini's principles does it exemplify?
options: Making a large initial request; illustrates the authority principle
Making a small initial request followed by a larger one; illustrates commitment/consistency
Offering a free sample of a product; illustrates the reciprocation principle
Emphasizing that an item is in short supply; illustrates the scarcity principle
Using a celebrity to endorse a product; illustrates the liking principle
questions.explain: The foot-in-the-door technique (得寸進尺法) involves first getting a small commitment, which then leads to greater compliance with a larger request. This works because people want to appear consistent with their earlier behaviour — a core feature of the commitment/consistency principle.

questions.q: How is obedience distinct from conformity and compliance?
options: Obedience involves matching group behaviour; conformity and compliance are individual responses
Obedience is adherence to commands from someone with higher status or authority
Obedience only occurs in laboratory settings, while conformity and compliance occur in everyday life
Obedience is unconscious, while conformity and compliance are conscious
Obedience affects more people than conformity or compliance
questions.explain: Obedience specifically involves following commands or instructions from someone with higher status or authority (Milgram's definition). This is distinct from conformity (matching peer group responses) and compliance (responding to requests from peers).

questions.q: In Milgram's shock experiment, what was the original predicted obedience rate by laypeople before the study began?
options: Approximately 10-15%
Approximately 35-40%
Approximately 60-70%
Almost no participant would deliver maximum shock
Nearly all participants would deliver maximum shock
questions.explain: Laypeople predicted that almost no participant would deliver the maximum shock, but the actual obedience rate was approximately 56%. This dramatic discrepancy between prediction and reality is what made Milgram's findings so shocking and important.

questions.q: What was the range of obedience rates across U.S. studies of the Milgram-type experiment?
options: Below 5%
questions.explain: U.S. studies of Milgram-type experiments ranged from 30% (Podd, 1970) to 91% (Ring et al., 1970), with a mean of approximately 61%. This variation shows that obedience is influenced by experimental conditions, not just blindly universal.

questions.q: According to Blass's (2012) cross-cultural review, how did obedience rates in non-U.S. countries compare to Milgram's original findings?
options: Foreign studies showed dramatically lower obedience rates
Foreign studies showed dramatically higher obedience rates
Average obedience scores were in roughly the same range regardless of culture
There was no data available from non-U.S. countries
Cultural differences made cross-cultural comparison impossible
questions.explain: Blass's cross-cultural review found that average obedience scores were in roughly the same range as Milgram's original findings regardless of culture — ranging from 28% (Australia) to 87.5% (South Africa), with a foreign mean of ~66%. The exam trap is thinking obedience is culture-specific when evidence shows consistency.

questions.q: In Burger's (2009) replication of Milgram's study, what was the effect of showing participants a model who defied the experimenter?
options: Defiance models had no substantial effect on obedience
Defiance models increased obedience substantially
Defiance models reduced obedience by more than 50 percentage points
Participants immediately stopped participating when they saw the model refuse
Models were not tested in the replication
questions.explain: In Burger's replication, seeing a defying model (someone who refused to continue) did not substantially reduce obedience. Base refusal condition showed 70% continued; modelled refusal condition showed 63.3% continued — only about a 7-point difference, suggesting that observing defiance does not dramatically increase the likelihood of one's own defiance.

questions.q: According to the lecture, what are the reasons that some participants chose to defy unjust authority in Milgram's study?
options: Fear of legal consequences and financial penalties
Worry about the performer's health, moral-ethical decisions, empathy, and situational incongruity
Disbelief that the study was real
Prior training in ethics and resistance
Pressure from family members to refuse
questions.explain: Bocchiaro & Zimbardo (2010) identified that defiers cited: (1) worry about the performer's health; (2) moral-ethical decision; (3) empathy; (4) situational incongruity (the situation did not fit their sense of right and wrong). These internal moral guides, not external consequences, motivated defiance.

questions.q: What is whistle-blowing in the context of social influence and obedience?
options: The act of following orders without question
Reporting ethically questionable orders to higher authorities
Making a loud noise to draw attention
Refusing to participate in a study
Informing the media about a workplace issue
questions.explain: Whistle-blowing (揭發) goes beyond individual defiance — it involves reporting ethically questionable orders to higher authorities. According to Bocchiaro et al. (2012), even fewer people engage in whistle-blowing than in defiance alone, making it the most morally courageous response.

questions.q: What is the difference between descriptive norms and injunctive/prescriptive norms in behaviour-change interventions?
options: Descriptive norms focus on rules; injunctive norms focus on suggestions
Descriptive norms describe what people do; injunctive norms describe what people approve of
Descriptive norms are newer; injunctive norms are outdated
Descriptive norms apply to individuals; injunctive norms apply to groups
They are synonymous terms used interchangeably
questions.explain: Descriptive norms convey what most people actually do (e.g., 'most people conserve water'). Injunctive/prescriptive norms convey what most people approve of (e.g., 'most people believe conserving water is important'). Both are used in interventions but work through different mechanisms.

questions.q: In the Burger & Shelton (2011) elevator vs. stairs study, what was the effect of the norm-sign?
options: The norm-sign had no effect on elevator use
Posting the norm-sign reduced elevator use by approximately 46%
Posting the norm-sign increased elevator use by 30%
The norm-sign only affected participants over age 40
The effect reversed after the sign was removed
questions.explain: Posting a descriptive norm sign ('more than 90% of the time, people in this building use the stairs') in Week 2 reduced elevator use by 46%, from approximately 15% to 8%. The effect demonstrates the power of descriptive norms in real-world behaviour change.

questions.q: How did the exercise-sign condition compare to the norm-sign condition in the Burger & Shelton study?
options: The exercise sign was more effective than the norm sign
The exercise sign had minimal impact across weeks
The exercise sign eliminated elevator use entirely
The exercise sign increased stair use by 90%
The two signs were equally effective
questions.explain: The exercise-sign condition (presumably focusing on health benefits) showed minimal change across weeks (~15.1%, 13.3%, 13.4%), whereas the norm-sign reduced use substantially. This illustrates that descriptive norm messages are more effective than health or environmental messaging alone.

questions.q: In the Goldstein et al. (2008) hotel towel study, what was the towel reuse rate when a descriptive norm message was used?
questions.explain: The descriptive norm message ('Almost 75% of guests reuse their towels') yielded a reuse rate of 44.1%, compared to 35.1% for a standard environmental protection message. The 9-percentage-point advantage demonstrates the practical power of descriptive norms in applied settings.

questions.q: Which of the following questions about social influence mechanisms would be most directly addressed by comparing the Burger & Shelton elevator study with the Goldstein et al. hotel study?
options: Whether group size affects obedience rates
Whether descriptive norm messages are effective across different contexts and behaviours
Whether automatic mimicry occurs in workplace settings
Whether authority figures are necessary for compliance
Whether informational influence differs by age group
questions.explain: Both studies tested descriptive norm interventions but in very different real-world contexts (stair use vs. towel reuse). Comparing them addresses the generalizability of descriptive norms — showing they work across diverse behaviours and settings, not just in laboratory conditions.

questions.q: In the conformity study examining political opinion, participants were more likely to answer 'Yes' to policy questions when group members also said 'Yes'. What does this finding suggest about the dominance of conformity mechanisms in political contexts?
options: Normative influence is eliminated entirely in political discussions
Informational influence completely overrides personal beliefs
People conform to group opinions on policy even without factual ambiguity, suggesting normative influence is prominent
Only extroverts exhibit conformity in political contexts
Political opinions are immune to social influence mechanisms
questions.explain: The political opinion conformity finding (38% conformity rate) demonstrates that normative influence is strong in political discussions even when there is no factual ambiguity — people care about social approval and group harmony, not just accuracy. This shows that conformity extends beyond ambiguous situations (where informational influence dominates) into value-based domains where normative influence is the primary driver.

questions.q: The foot-in-the-door technique ('得寸進尺法') is an example of the commitment/consistency principle. Why does committing to a small initial action increase compliance with a subsequent larger request?
options: Large requests are inherently easier than small requests
People want to appear consistent with their earlier publicly stated behaviour and sense of self
Authority figures are more effective when they ask multiple times
The compliance rate increases regardless of what the initial request was
Small initial actions exhaust people's ability to refuse
questions.explain: The foot-in-the-door technique works through the commitment/consistency principle: once people have made a small commitment and acted on it, they want to see themselves as consistent (and have others see them as consistent) with that behaviour. A larger follow-up request activates this desire to remain consistent with the earlier action, making refusal feel like it would contradict their self-image.

questions.q: Which of the following scenarios best illustrates the difference between informational and normative influence in a real-world decision?
options: A person answers a quiz question identically to others because they believe the group's answer is factually correct (informational) vs. a person answers identically because they fear peer disapproval if they disagree (normative)
Automatic mimicry occurs vs. conscious deliberation occurs
Conformity happens in ambiguous situations vs. conformity happens in clear situations
Obedience to authority occurs vs. compliance with peer requests occurs
Defiance leads to whistle-blowing vs. defiance remains silent
questions.explain: Informational influence is when someone conforms because they genuinely believe the group is correct (accuracy-driven). Normative influence is when someone conforms because they want approval or to avoid disapproval (approval-driven). The scenario clearly separates the two mechanisms: informational = 'I conform because I think they're right'; normative = 'I conform because I don't want to be disliked.'
